Original instructions

Quick start About this manual

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document for the STEPFOC stepper driver. It is revised as the product and its firmware change; the document number, firmware version, revision and date above identify the version you are reading, and the document history on the About page says what changed. Take care that the firmware version named under Applies to matches what #Info reports on your driver: the version selector in the header switches between firmware releases. The text and the images are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples MIT.

Reset view

Drag to turn the board, scroll to zoom. The model is the board's STEP file from the repository, the PCB and everything mounted on it.

    Four short parts from the box to a calibrated motor that follows commands, through Motor GUI or the terminal, with a link into the manual at every step.

  • Learn

    Guides with code, the bootloader, and the theory corner on FOC, the cascade and impedance control.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: STEPFOC is a bare circuit board that drives a motor from a supply of up to 29 V. Read this chapter before you connect anything; the few rules here are the ones that destroy a driver, a motor or a finger when they are ignored.

docs.title: Electrical
docs.text:
Supply polarity

Reversing the polarity on DC+ and DC− destroys the driver at once. Check the polarity of every power cable before you plug it in, every time.

Cable orientation on the daisy chain

The CAN and power cables that link one driver to the next are keyed by their orientation, not by their connector: a cable plugged in the wrong way round puts the supply on the wrong pins and destroys the driver. Use the cables from the Source Robotics shop, or make yours exactly as shown in Power and the CAN daisy chain.

UART is 3.3 V

The UART port runs at 3.3 V. A 5 V serial adapter destroys the board. Use a 3.3 V adapter, such as the one from the shop.

Supply voltage

12 to 29 V DC. The driver raises a Vbus error below 9 V and above 29 V (#Vmax, 29000 mV after #Default), and 29 V is also the hardware limit: do not connect a supply that can rise above it, and allow for the voltage a decelerating motor pushes back into the supply. A bench supply with a current limit is the safest way to start.

Do not disconnect a running motor

Never unplug a motor, or a power cable in the daisy chain, while the driver is powered. The inductive kick of the coils and the arcing at the connector damage the driver stage.

Static electricity

Static electricity damages the microcontroller, the encoder chip and the driver stage. Unplug the supply and touch earthed metal before you handle the board, and hold it by its edges, away from the chips and the pads.

docs.title: Mechanical
docs.text:
Moving parts

A calibrating or running motor turns without warning, in both directions, and the stepper in position mode pushes back hard against a hand. Keep fingers, hair and cables away from the shaft and whatever is mounted on it, fix the motor to the bench before the first test, and test without a load on the shaft.

A powered motor can move with nobody at it

The driver moves its motor whenever a command arrives, over UART or from any host on the CAN bus, and keeps following the last one. From firmware 109 it also turns the motor by itself for about a minute after a calibration, to measure the encoder table and the anti-cogging. A speed command goes on turning the motor after the program that sent it has crashed or its cable has come out, unless the watchdog is set (Stopping the motor). Before you reach for the motor or the mechanism it drives, put the driver in idle (#Idle, Send_Idle) or switch the supply off.

The encoder magnet

The magnet sits about 1 mm above the encoder chip. A magnet that touches the chip, or sits far too close, can damage the microcontroller; a magnet too far away gives a wrong position. Mount it as described in The encoder magnet.

Hot motor and driver

A stepper running at its rated current gets hot enough to burn, and so do the driver's chips and the board around them. Switch off and let both cool for a few minutes before you touch them. Set the current limit for your motor (Current limit and loop tuning), use the thermistor, and give the driver airflow when it runs near 2.8 A. From firmware 109 #Ilim, the current limit of Send_Limits over CAN and the current of a gripper move all stop at 2800 mA. A host must still keep them within the motor's rating.

docs.title: Stopping the motor
docs.text:
• Send_ESTOP over CAN, or #Idle over UART, stops the motor at once; the E-stop error stays until it is cleared.
  • Cutting the supply stops the motor as well; a stepper then holds nothing, so a vertical axis drops.
  • The watchdog (Send_Watchdog) stops the motor by itself when the host stops talking. From firmware 109 its action can instead hold the position or let a joint down at a limited speed, for a set time at most, then brake or coast (The watchdog): while that runs the motor is still driven.

Nothing on the driver is a certified safety function. A machine that can hurt someone needs an emergency stop that cuts the motor supply, independent of the driver.

docs.title: Firmware updates and programming
docs.text: When you connect a programming adapter to the JTAG connector, disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter first. Updating over the bootloader needs no adapter; see Firmware.

docs.title: Liability
docs.text: STEPFOC is sold as a component for people who build their own machines. Its hardware designs, firmware and this documentation are under development and may contain errors. Whoever builds a machine with it is responsible for its safe design, assembly and operation.

docs.title: Scope and audience
docs.text:
The STEPFOC Manual covers the STEPFOC stepper driver from unpacking to a tuned motor on a CAN bus: what the driver is, how to mount it on a motor and wire it, the first setup over the serial terminal, calibration and tuning, how the driver is controlled over UART and CAN or from Python, and how its firmware is updated. The Reference lists every CAN message and UART command of the firmware release named on the landing page. The Guides are worked examples.

It is written for someone who builds a robot or a machine with STEPFOC: a maker, a student or an engineer who can solder four motor wires and open a serial terminal. It does not assume any knowledge of field-oriented control; the Theory corner in the appendix explains the concepts the control modes rely on.

Read the Safety chapter before you power anything. The Quick start is the whole first setup, in four short parts; the chapters are in the order you need them and go deeper.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
The header has four tabs. STEPFOC Manual is the document you read from the start: the quick start, then safety, technical data, mounting, the first setup, operation and firmware updates, in numbered chapters. Motor GUI, the tool in the browser, is the usual way to do what the chapters describe; each procedure shows it first and the terminal command beside it. API reference lists every CAN message, every UART command and the Python library's calls for the firmware release this site describes, with the defaults and the error flags, and is where you look things up. Guides are worked examples with code. Support says where to get help and how to report a problem.

The whole site describes one firmware release. The dropdown next to the site name switches between releases, and a page from an older release says so in a bar at the top. The repository card on the right of the header opens the firmware repository; every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report a problem with it.

docs.title: Warnings and notes
docs.text:
Three kinds of highlighted text appear in this documentation. Read every Danger and Notice before you act on the step it belongs to.

Note

Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

Notice

The driver, the motor, the machine or data can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

Danger

Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Activated A flag the driver keeps (#Activate, Send_gripper_data_pack). In gripper mode a move is carried out only while the gripper is activated. ADDITIONAL2 A spare pin of the driver, usable as an analog input or a digital input/output. HALL mode homes the motor against a sensor wired to it. Angle offset (theta offset) The angle between the encoder's zero and the motor's electrical zero, found by calibration and stored. The driver needs it to place the current vector relative to the rotor. Anti-cogging A current added to the current setpoint, a function of the electrical angle, that cancels the motor's own torque ripple (its pull towards the detents and the ripple of current-sensing errors). Identified on the driver (#Cogcal, parameter 43). Back-EMF The voltage a turning motor generates in its own coils, proportional to speed. It opposes the supply, limits the top speed at a given voltage. Calibration estimates KV from the speed the motor reaches per volt. Board ID The bootloader's own address, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. Saving the configuration (#Save) writes the CAN node ID into it. Bootloader The program in the first 12 KB of the driver's flash on boards shipped with firmware 105 or newer, and on some shipped before. It starts the firmware, and loads a new firmware over UART or CAN. See The bootloader. Calibration The routine (#Cal) that checks the magnet and the supply, takes the motor's resistance, inductance and pole pairs, computes the current loop gains, spins the motor in open loop to learn the wiring, finds the angle offset and measures Kt, KV and the flux linkage. Its result is kept with #Save. CAN ID (node ID) The address of the driver on the CAN bus, 0 to 13 (the bootloader reserves 14 and 15). It occupies bits 10 to 7 of the 11-bit CAN frame identifier; the command ID occupies bits 6 to 1 and the error bit is bit 0. CANvas Source Robotics' USB-to-CAN adapter. It appears as a serial port and speaks slcan, which python-can and Motor GUI use. Command ID The number, 0 to 63, in bits 6 to 1 of a CAN frame identifier that says which message the frame carries. The API reference lists every command ID. Commutation Placing the stator current so that it produces torque at the rotor's present angle. FOC does it continuously from the encoder angle and the angle offset; a conventional stepper driver does it blindly, step by step. Commutation delay compensation (parameter 64) Turning the output voltage forward by the angle the rotor covers between the angle reading and the moment the voltage reaches the motor. 166 µs on STEPFOC by default. Control mode What the driver is doing with the motor: idle, position, velocity, current, PD (impedance), voltage torque, open loop, HALL, gripper, or calibration. A command that carries a setpoint puts the driver in the matching mode. Current loop bandwidth (#Cbw, parameter 49) How fast the current loop follows a change of its setpoint, in Hz. The current loop gains follow from it and the motor's resistance and inductance: Kp = ω·L, Ki = ω·R. The firmware keeps Ki per control loop: Kiiq is about ω·R × 160 µs. 160 Hz by default from firmware 109. Current-sense zero The reading of a current sensor with no current flowing. From firmware 109 the driver measures it at every start-up and subtracts it; the anti-cogging identification can trim it further. d-q frame The rotating frame of reference FOC works in: the q axis is at right angles to the rotor field and the current on it (Iq) produces torque; the d axis is along the field and its current (Id) produces none, so it is held at 0. Daisy chain Several drivers on one CAN bus and one supply, each driver's second CAN and power connector feeding the next. Diametrical magnet A disc magnet whose poles are across its diameter, so the field turns with the shaft. The encoder needs this kind; an axially magnetised disc looks the same and does not work. EEPROM The non-volatile memory on the driver that holds the configuration and the calibration. #Save writes it, #Default restores the factory values. Encoder table A correction of the encoder's small angle error around the turn, measured on the driver (#Encal, parameter 52) and saved with the configuration. Encoder ticks The unit of position: the 14-bit magnetic encoder gives 16384 ticks per revolution of the motor shaft, counted over as many revolutions as the motor makes. Speed is in ticks per second. Error bit Bit 0 of every CAN frame identifier the driver sends: 1 while any error is active. Feedforward A term added to a loop's output from what is known in advance rather than from the error: the motion frames carry a speed and a current feedforward so a host that knows the trajectory can command it directly, leaving the loops to correct the rest. Field-oriented control (FOC) Controlling a motor by regulating the stator current as a vector in the rotor's frame, from a measurement of the rotor angle. On a stepper it replaces the fixed step currents with sinusoidal currents that follow the rotor, which gives smooth, quiet, efficient motion with no lost steps and a known position. Firmware release One build of the firmware, numbered 103, 105, 106, … and tagged V103, V105, … in the firmware repository. #Info prints the release a driver runs. This documentation describes one release; the version selector switches between them. Flux linkage The rotor's magnetic flux as seen by a coil, in weber; calibration computes it from Kt. Gripper mode The driver running a gripper (#Gripper 1): jaw positions from 0 (open) to 255 (closed), a speed, a current limit that becomes the grip force, and object detection. HALL mode Homing against a sensor on ADDITIONAL2: the motor turns at a set speed until the sensor triggers, then holds the position reached. With a level trigger it holds only while the pin stays at that level. Heartbeat A frame (Respond_Heartbeat) the driver sends at a set interval so the host knows it is alive. Off by default. Impedance (PD) mode The control mode in which the driver behaves like a spring and a damper around a position setpoint, with the stiffness KP and the damping KD, plus a current feedforward. Iq, Id The two components of the motor current in the d-q frame: Iq produces torque, Id is normally held at 0. The current mode's setpoint and limit are Iq values. Kt, KV The motor's torque constant (torque per ampere) and velocity constant (speed per volt), found by calibration. Kt turns a current into an estimated torque; KV gives the top speed at a supply voltage. Microstepping Driving a stepper with intermediate current levels between full steps. Only the open-loop commands (#gosteps, #microstep) use it; under FOC the current follows the rotor continuously. Motor GUI Source Robotics' browser tool for the driver: tuning, plots and firmware updates over a serial or CAN adapter. Open loop Driving the motor as a plain stepper, without the encoder in the loop: #Openloop, #gosteps, and the open-loop spin of the calibration. Parameter A setting reached by its number through Send_Parameter and Send_Get_Parameter (CAN 36 to 38) or #Par (firmware 109 and newer). The numbers are permanent. Phase order How the stepper's two coils are connected to A+/A− and B+/B−. Firmware 105 and newer learns the wiring during calibration and compensates it; firmware 103 asks for the wires to be swapped when it is reversed. PLL (speed estimate) A phase-locked loop that follows the encoder count and gives the speed with less lag than a moving average. The default speed estimate of STEPFOC from firmware 109 (parameter 50). Pole pairs The number of electrical cycles per mechanical revolution: 50 for a 1.8° stepper, 100 for a 0.9° stepper. Set with #PP before calibration. Product lock The stamp in the EEPROM of the product that calibrated a board. A firmware that finds the other product's stamp drives nothing (firmware 109 and newer). Remote frame A CAN frame with the RTR bit set and no data: a request. The host asks for data with a remote frame under a command ID, and the driver answers with a data frame under the same ID. Sound (#Tone, CAN 44 and 45) Tones, a queue of notes and recorded samples the driver adds to its output voltage while it holds or moves, so the motor plays them (firmware 109 and newer). Spectral Micro Source Robotics' BLDC driver, STEPFOC's sister: similar hardware and firmware and practically the same commands, for three-phase brushless motors. Step angle The angle of one full step of a stepper: 1.8° for the common 200-step motor, 0.9° for a 400-step motor. It sets the pole pairs: 360 ÷ (4 × step angle). Termination The 120 Ω resistor the first and the last node of a CAN bus need. The switch on the driver turns it on. Tool id (#Tool, parameter 1) What a drive is built into: 0 none, 1 SSG-48, 11 to 33 an MSG, 200 to 254 a customer's tool. Vbus The supply voltage at the driver, measured and printed in mV. Outside the limits the driver raises a Vbus error. Watchdog A timer the driver resets with every motion frame and every status request it answers. When it is set (Send_Watchdog) and runs out, the driver reports a watchdog error and stops; from firmware 109 it holds, brakes, coasts or descends as the watchdog's action says.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: What STEPFOC is and what it is made of, how it relates to the Spectral Micro BLDC driver it is built on, and what you need around it to get a motor turning.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• The driver at a glance
  • STEPFOC and Spectral Micro
  • What you need

docs.title: The driver at a glance
docs.text:
STEPFOC is a field-oriented controller for bipolar stepper motors. It sits on the back of a NEMA 17 motor, reads the rotor position from a magnet on the motor shaft, and drives the two coils with sinusoidal currents the way a servo drive does, instead of the fixed step currents of a conventional stepper driver.

The result is a stepper that runs quietly and efficiently, never loses steps, reports its position, and can be commanded in position, speed, current (torque) or impedance.

Figure 1.1: The STEPFOC driver, 39 × 39 mm, with the encoder chip in the middle of the board.

docs.title: What is on the board
docs.text:
Part What it does STM32F103CB microcontroller runs the control loops at 6250 Hz and the CAN and UART interfaces 14-bit magnetic encoder (MT6816) reads the position of the magnet on the motor shaft: 16384 ticks per revolution H-bridge driver with inline current sensing drives the two coils with up to 2.8 A and measures the phase currents 16 Kbit EEPROM keeps the configuration and the calibration over a power cycle Two CAN connectors and two power connectors daisy-chain several drivers on one bus and one supply CAN termination switch the 120 Ω resistor the first and the last node need UART connector (3.3 V) the serial terminal: every setting, calibration, tuning Thermistor connector an NTC on the motor for temperature protection ADDITIONAL2 pin an input or output you can use: HALL mode homes against a sensor wired here JTAG pads (1.27 mm) the programming adapter, for installing the bootloader or for development Status LED normal operation, calibration or error, see below

The connectors and their pinout are in Connectors and pinout.

docs.title: What the firmware does
docs.text:
The firmware closes three nested loops on the motor: a current (torque) loop, a velocity loop around it and a position loop around that, plus an impedance (PD) loop that makes the motor behave like a spring and damper.

A command picks the loop: a current setpoint, a speed, a position or a PD setpoint. Open-loop stepping, a voltage-torque mode and a homing mode against a sensor exist beside them; Control modes describes each.

The driver protects itself and the motor: it stops on a supply voltage outside the limits, on an encoder fault (no magnet), on a motor over-temperature (with the thermistor), on an E-stop command and on a watchdog that runs out.

The status LED and #Error tell which; see Errors and recovery. It does not monitor its driver stage: a fault there is not reported.

docs.title: How it is controlled
docs.text:
• UART, a 3.3 V serial port at 256000 baud: human-readable commands such as #P 16384, and the only way to run the calibration. See Over UART.
  • CAN, 1 Mbit/s, up to 14 drivers on one bus (node IDs 0 to 13): compact frames for real-time control from a PC with the CANvas adapter, a microcontroller or a robot control box. See Over CAN.
  • Python, the Spectral-BLDC library on top of CAN. See With Python.
  • Motor GUI, in the browser, over serial or CAN: the usual tool for setup, testing and tuning. See Motor GUI.

docs.title: The status LED
docs.text:
Pattern Meaning three short flashes and a pause normal operation: no error, calibrated fast flashing, about ten times a second the calibration routine is running on, not flashing error mode: at least one error is active, or the motor is not calibrated

The LED can be turned off with #LED 0.

Normal operation Calibration Error mode

docs.title: STEPFOC and Spectral Micro
docs.text:
STEPFOC and the Spectral Micro BLDC driver are sister drivers: similar hardware and similar firmware, each made for its kind of motor. The Spectral Micro drives three-phase brushless motors; STEPFOC drives two-phase stepper motors.

They are not the same board and do not run the same firmware, but they are controlled and run practically the same way: the same CAN and UART commands, the same Python library, Motor GUI and bootloader.

What this means in practice:

  • The commands are practically the same. The CAN messages and UART commands of the Reference have the same IDs, names and layouts on both drivers; STEPFOC adds a few that only make sense on a stepper (homing against a sensor, open-loop stepping). A program written for one runs on the other.
  • The firmware releases go in step, and from 109 share their numbers. A change that applies to both drivers comes to both. From release 109 they are released together under the same version number; the Spectral Micro went from 107 straight to 109, so there is no Spectral Micro 108. Before, the numbers did not always match (STEPFOC 108 went with Spectral Micro 107); the compatibility table lists the pairs.
  • Calibration differs. A BLDC driver measures the motor's resistance and inductance and finds its pole pairs; STEPFOC cannot, so you enter the three values from the motor's datasheet before calibrating. See Motor parameters and calibration. From firmware 109 #Cal is followed by the encoder table and the anti-cogging on both drivers.
  • Some defaults differ. Each driver's were measured on its own bench: the direct PLL speed estimate at 60 Hz and 166 µs delay compensation here, 100 Hz and 234 µs on the Spectral Micro; velocity gains 0.02 / 0.001 here, 0.03 / 0.0003 there. STEPFOC brakes in idle by default, the Spectral Micro coasts.
  • The motor terminals differ. A+, A−, B+, B− for the two stepper coils instead of U, V, W.
  • Some images on this site show a Spectral Micro. Where a photo or a screenshot shows the BLDC board, the procedure is the same for STEPFOC.

The guides under the Guides tab were written with the Spectral Micro; the code in them runs unchanged on STEPFOC.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: This page lists what a STEPFOC setup is made of, what comes with the driver, and what you buy or make yourself.

docs.title: The driver
docs.text:
STEPFOC is sold as a single driver or as a starter kit in the Source Robotics shop:

  • STEPFOC stepper driver
  • STEPFOC starter kit, which adds the adapters, the magnet, the cables and a thermistor listed below

Every driver is end-of-line tested and ships with the current firmware release and the bootloader already installed, so a driver works out of the box with a serial terminal, the Python library or Motor GUI. The firmware can be updated later without a programming adapter; see Firmware.

docs.title: A stepper motor
docs.text: STEPFOC drives bipolar (4-wire) stepper motors. It is made for the NEMA 17 frame, whose mounting holes match the board; it also works with NEMA 23 motors on the NEMA 23 spacer, and with other frames on an adapter you make. Look for a motor with a phase resistance of 1 to 5 Ω and a rated current of 3 A or less; the tested motors are known to work.

docs.title: The encoder magnet
docs.text: A diametrically magnetised 6 × 2.5 mm neodymium magnet on the rear of the motor shaft, about 1 mm above the encoder chip in the middle of the board: 6 × 2.5 mm diametrical magnet. An axially magnetised magnet, or one that wobbles, makes calibration fail or report bad positions. The 6 × 2.5 mm size is the stock one, not a requirement: another thickness is a way to set the 1 mm gap when a shaft or a spacer leaves the wrong distance. The encoder magnet says how to fit it.

docs.title: Adapters and cables
docs.text:
Part Needed for Shop USB-to-serial adapter (3.3 V) the serial terminal: calibration, tuning, any # command Serial adapter CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter CAN control from a PC, the Python library, Motor GUI over CAN CAN adapter CAN cable and power cable daisy-chaining several drivers CAN cable, power cable 100 kΩ NTC thermistor motor temperature protection (optional but recommended) Thermistor JTAG programming adapter only for installing the bootloader on an older board, or for firmware development Programming adapter

Cable orientation

The daisy-chain cables for CAN and power are keyed by their orientation, not by their connector. A cable plugged in the wrong way round destroys the driver. Use the cables from the shop or follow Power and the CAN daisy chain exactly when you make your own.

docs.title: A power supply
docs.text: 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V recommended; see Ratings and limits. Calibrate at 24 V. From firmware 109 the motor constants no longer depend on the supply: the spins that measure them run at their own 6 V limit. A bench supply with a current limit is the safest way to start.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
• Motor GUI, in the browser, over the serial adapter or the CAN adapter: the usual tool for setup, calibration, tuning, plots and firmware updates; see Motor GUI.
  • Or a serial terminal: PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor in VS Code, or the Arduino serial monitor; see The serial terminal.
  • The Python library Spectral-BLDC for CAN control from your own programs; see With Python.

docs.title: Connectors and pinout
docs.text:
Figure 3.1: The connectors. The motor coils go to A+, A−, B+, B−; the supply to DC+ and DC−. Connector Pins Type Cable Motor A+, A−, B+, B− solder pads the motor's own leads, see Wiring the stepper Power, two of them DC+, DC− JST XH, 2 pins Power cable; the second connector feeds the next driver CAN, two of them CAN L, CAN H JST ZH, 2 pins CAN cable; the second connector feeds the next driver UART 3.3 V, TX, RX, GND JST SH, 4 pins UART cable Thermistor NTC, NTC JST SH, 2 pins the 100 kΩ NTC from the shop or any 100 kΩ NTC JTAG 3.3 V, GND, SWCLK, SWDIO pads, 1.27 mm pitch Programming adapter, pressed onto the pads; the order is marked in Installing the bootloader ADDITIONAL2 signal, GND pads your sensor; the HALL homing mode reads this pin STEP / DIR STEP, DIR, GND, 24 V header hardware only: the firmware does not support a step/dir interface

Polarity and orientation

DC+ to the positive supply, DC− to the negative; a cable the wrong way round destroys the driver. The daisy-chain cables have an orientation too: see Power and the CAN daisy chain.

Note

  • UART is TX to RX and RX to TX between the driver and the adapter.
  • The UART port and the ADDITIONAL2 pin are 3.3 V. 5 V on either destroys the board.
  • The thermistor pin has a 54.9 kΩ pull-down; the firmware's temperature table is for a 100 kΩ NTC.
  • The CAN termination switch is next to the CAN connectors; ON connects the 120 Ω resistor.

docs.title: Dimensions and CAD
docs.text:
The board is 39 × 39 mm with the four mounting holes on the NEMA 17 pattern (31 mm apart), so it bolts to the back of a NEMA 17 motor with the motor's own screws and a spacer. The encoder chip is exactly in the middle of the board, on the motor shaft's axis.

Reset view

Drag to turn the board, scroll to zoom. The model is the board's STEP file from the repository, the PCB and everything mounted on it.

Figure 3.2: Board dimensions and hole pattern. The drawing is of the Spectral Micro, which has the same outline and hole pattern. Figure 3.3: The board's model, from its STEP file: the PCB and everything mounted on it.

The STEP files of the board, the magnet spacers for different motor lengths and the tool for pressing the magnet onto the shaft are in the firmware repository:

  • STEP files of the board
  • Stepper motor accessories: magnet spacers, NEMA 17 spacers for different motor lengths, NEMA 23 spacers
  • Tools: the magnet tool

Downloads and files lists everything that can be downloaded.

docs.title: Electrical
docs.text:
Value Supply voltage 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V typical Vbus error limits (firmware) below 9 V or above 29 V (#Vmax, 29000 mV after #Default) Phase current, continuous 1.5 A typical Phase current, maximum 2.8 A; needs good cooling and short bursts. #Ilim is clamped to 2800 mA, and from firmware 109 so is Send_Limits over CAN Current limit, default 1700 mA after #Default; calibration uses 1600 mA for its steps and, from firmware 109, puts the limit back Power, maximum 80 W Power, idle 0.3 W PWM frequency 25 kHz Control loop frequency 6250 Hz Electrical frequency, maximum 600 Hz Current sensing inline, both phases Encoder 14-bit magnetic, 16384 ticks per revolution, diametrical magnet 1 mm above the chip UART 3.3 V, 256000 baud by default (1 000 000 tested) CAN CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers, node IDs 0 to 13 (the bootloader reserves 14 and 15), 120 Ω termination by switch Thermistor input 100 kΩ NTC, 54.9 kΩ pull-down ADDITIONAL2 analog input or general-purpose input/output, 3.3 V Driver stage protection not monitored: the firmware reads no fault output of the driver stage, and its driver error flag stays 0

Polarity

Reversing the polarity on DC+ and DC− destroys the board.

docs.title: Thermal and environmental
docs.text: Value Operating temperature of the board −20 to 130 °C Motor temperature limit (firmware, with the thermistor) 75 °C by default (#Tlim), −20 °C minimum

docs.text:
Value Position signed 24-bit over CAN (±8.4 million ticks, ±512 revolutions), 32-bit internally Speed signed 24-bit over CAN, encoder ticks per second Current setpoint signed 16-bit over CAN, mA Pole pairs accepted by calibration 50, 75, 100 or 125 Configuration kept in the EEPROM with #Save / Send_Save_config

The defaults of every setting are listed in the Defaults reference.

docs.title: Tested motors
docs.text:
STEPFOC works with bipolar (4-wire) stepper motors whose phase resistance is 1 to 5 Ω and whose rated current is 3 A or less. The motors below have been run on it; the resistance and inductance are the datasheet values of one coil, which is what you enter with #R and #L before calibration.

Motor Frame Pole pairs Phase resistance Phase inductance Rated current Mass 17HS08-1004S NEMA 17, 20 mm 50 3.7 Ω 4.5 mH 1.0 A 140 g Stepperonline 17HS16-2004S1 NEMA 17, 40 mm 50 1.1 Ω 2.6 mH 2.0 A 310 g Stepperonline 17HS24-2104S NEMA 17, 60 mm 50 1.6 Ω 3.0 mH 2.1 A 500 g Stepperonline 23HM22-2804S NEMA 23, 56 mm, 0.9° 100 1.16 Ω 4.2 mH 2.8 A 700 g Stepperonline

Before calibration, set the current limit to the motor's rated current with #Ilim: it is 1700 mA after #Default, more than the 17HS08's rating, and the encoder table that follows a calibration runs at 80 % of it.

Calibration uses its own 1600 mA for its steps and puts your limit back when it ends. See Current limit and loop tuning.

Choosing a motor

A lower phase resistance and inductance give a higher speed at a given supply voltage; the velocity constant KV that calibration finds tells how fast the motor can turn: roughly 0.8 × V × KV revolutions per minute, where V is the voltage limit #Vlim (6 V by default) or the supply voltage, whichever is lower. Motors with visibly uneven windings or a resistance that differs between the two coils calibrate badly.

docs.title: Mounting and wiring
docs.text:
How the driver goes onto the motor and what gets connected to it: the encoder magnet on the shaft, the board on the motor's back, the two coils to the motor terminals, the supply and the CAN bus, and the thermistor. Do the pages in order; the magnet first, because it is the one thing you cannot check from the outside later.

Figure 4.1: The motor hardware setup video shows the whole procedure on a NEMA 17 motor.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• The encoder magnet
  • Mounting on the motor
  • Wiring the stepper
  • Power and the CAN daisy chain
  • Thermistor

When all of it is done, continue with First setup.

docs.title: The encoder magnet
docs.text:
The encoder reads a diametrically magnetised magnet on the rear end of the motor shaft. The magnet must sit centred on the shaft's axis, parallel to the board, about 1 mm above the encoder chip, and it must not move.

Figure 4.2: About 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip in the middle of the board.

docs.title: The magnet
docs.text:
A neodymium disc, diametrically magnetised (north and south across the diameter, not through the thickness). The shop's 6 × 2.5 mm diametrical magnet is the size the printed spacers are made for. An axially magnetised magnet looks the same and does not work: the magnet test may even pass, and the position is wrong.

The size is not fixed

6 × 2.5 mm is the stock size, not a requirement. Any diametrically magnetised disc of about 6 mm diameter works, and the thickness is a way to set the gap: a thicker magnet brings its face closer to the encoder, a thinner one farther, so with a shaft or a spacer that leaves the wrong distance you can pick the thickness that gives 1 mm instead of changing the spacer. What matters is the 1 mm from the magnet's face to the chip, the magnet centred on the shaft, and the diametrical magnetisation.

docs.title: Fitting it
docs.text:
1. The motor needs a rear shaft. Most NEMA 17 motors have one; a motor without it needs a magnet holder on the front shaft and a different mechanical layout.
  2. Press the magnet onto the shaft centred. The magnet tool in the firmware repository is a printed jig that centres it; a 3D-printed magnet spacer from Stepper motor accessories fits between the shaft and the magnet when the shaft is too short.
  3. Fix it with a drop of glue. A magnet that can turn on the shaft is the classic cause of a calibration that reports success and a motor that then runs badly: the magnet slipped between calibration and use.
  4. Check the height after the board is mounted: with the spacer for your motor length, the gap is 1 mm. A magnet that touches the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet 2 mm away or more gives a weak signal.

Check

The magnet sits centred on the shaft, and once the glue has set it does not move when you push it with a finger.

docs.title: Checking it
docs.text:
With the driver powered and the serial terminal open, #Magnet answers Magnet Good when the chip sees enough field, Magnet Bad when it does not. The calibration routine runs the same test first.

What the magnet test checks

Only that a magnet is close enough to the encoder. It passes with a magnet that is not glued, sits off-centre or can slip on the shaft, and fails only when there is no magnet or it is too far away. The 1 mm gap, the centring and the glue are yours to check.

docs.title: Mounting on the motor
docs.text:
The board has the NEMA 17 hole pattern (31 mm), so it mounts on the back of the motor with the motor's own four rear screws, with a spacer between the motor and the board that sets the magnet height.

  1. Remove the four rear screws of the motor. They hold the motor's end cap; it does not come apart when you remove them one at a time and put the spacer and the board on at once.
  2. Put the spacer on the motor. The firmware repository has printable spacers for common motor lengths in Stepper motor accessories (NEMA 17, a 21.5 mm NEMA 17 version, NEMA 23); for another motor, make a spacer that leaves 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip.
  3. Put the board on the spacer, encoder chip towards the magnet, and fit longer screws of the same thread (M3 on a NEMA 17). Tighten them evenly; the board must be parallel to the magnet.
  4. Check the gap between the magnet and the encoder chip: about 1 mm, the magnet not touching it.

Check

The board sits parallel to the back of the motor, with about 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip, and the shaft turns by hand without the magnet touching the chip. If the gap is wrong: The encoder magnet.

A NEMA 23 motor takes the NEMA 23 spacer from the same folder. A smaller frame, such as NEMA 14, needs an adapter plate you make yourself: the repository has none.

The board is bare

Nothing on the back of the board may touch the motor's housing. Make sure the spacer keeps the board clear of the end cap, and keep metal swarf and screws away from the board while you work. Touch earthed metal before you pick the board up and hold it by its edges: static electricity damages its chips.

docs.title: Power and the CAN daisy chain
docs.text:
Each driver has two power connectors (JST XH) and two CAN connectors (JST ZH). The second connector of each pair feeds the next driver, so a chain of drivers hangs on one supply cable and one CAN cable.

Figure 4.4: Power and CAN pass from driver to driver. The first and the last node on the bus have their termination switch on.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
• 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V recommended. DC+ to the positive supply, DC− to the negative; reversed polarity destroys the driver.
  • The power connectors are rated for 4 A. A chain of drivers shares that: with motors at 1.5 A each, plan for at most two or three drivers per chain that draw their full current at the same time, and feed a longer chain from both ends or from several supplies.
  • A motor that decelerates pushes energy back into the supply. A lab supply or a battery absorbs it; a supply that cannot (some switch-mode supplies) sees its voltage rise, and the driver raises a Vbus error above 29 V (#Vmax).

docs.title: The cable orientation
docs.text:
Danger

The daisy-chain cables are keyed by their orientation, not by the connector: the same 2-pin cable fits both ways, and the wrong way puts DC+ on DC−. Every cable must run as in the picture below, the same way at both ends. A wrong cable destroys the driver at the moment it is powered.

Figure 4.5: The orientation of the daisy-chain cables, the same for the 2-pin power and CAN cables.

The cables from the shop are made this way: CAN cable, power cable, and all of them under connectors and cables.

docs.title: CAN
docs.text:
• CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers. Up to 14 drivers on one bus, each with its own node ID, 0 to 13 (0 by default; set it with #CANID or Send_CAN_ID and save). The firmware accepts 14 and 15 too, but the bootloader reserves them: a driver on one of those IDs cannot be updated over CAN.
  • Twisted-pair wire; keep the bus short at 1 Mbit/s (a few metres at most).
  • Termination: the first and the last node on the bus need a 120 Ω resistor between CAN H and CAN L. The switch next to the CAN connectors turns the driver's resistor on (ON). Drivers in the middle stay off. A bus with the right termination measures about 60 Ω between CAN H and CAN L with everything unpowered.
  • A PC joins the bus with the CANvas adapter, which has its own termination.
Figure 4.6: The termination switch, ON for the first and the last node.

docs.title: Thermistor
docs.text:
A 100 kΩ NTC thermistor on the motor lets the driver stop before the motor overheats. It is optional, and off by default; use it on any motor that runs near its rated current for long.

Without it, nothing protects the motor from overheating

The driver limits the current, not the temperature. A motor that runs continuously, holds a load for long, or is set up badly (a current limit above its rating, loops that oscillate, a wrong resistance or inductance) can overheat and burn its windings without any warning. With the thermistor fitted and enabled, the driver stops first. The starter kit includes one.

Figure 4.7: The thermistor on its 2-pin connector.

docs.title: Fitting it
docs.text:
A stepper is sealed: the windings cannot be reached.

Place the thermistor on the motor housing, as close to the windings as possible: either glued to the side of the housing, or in one of the four screw holes of the motor's bottom with the screw removed, which puts it deep in the stack. Thermal cement holds it and conducts the heat.

Figure 4.8: Thermal cement: it sets hard and conducts heat. Thermal paste stays soft and lets the bead move, ordinary glue insulates it. Where to buy it.

The housing lags behind the windings by some seconds, and reads lower. Set the limit with that in mind: the default of 75 °C at the housing corresponds to a hotter winding.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
#Term 1
#Tlim 75
#Save

#Temp then prints the temperature; with the thermistor disabled it prints Temp Off. Above the limit the driver raises a temperature error and stops; it clears with #Clear once the motor has cooled.

Over CAN, Send_Respond_Temperature returns the temperature, and the temperature error is one of the bits of Send_Respond_State_of_Errors.

docs.title: Wiring the stepper
docs.text:
A bipolar stepper has two coils and four wires. One coil goes to the terminals A+ and A−, the other to B+ and B−. Which coil is A and which is B does not matter, and neither does the polarity of each coil: firmware 105 and newer finds the wiring during calibration and compensates it.

Figure 4.3: The motor terminals A+, A−, B+, B− and the other connectors.

docs.title: Finding the two coils
docs.text:
On most stepper motors the colours give the pairs away: black and green are one coil, red and blue the other. The Stepperonline motors of Tested motors are wired that way: black to A+, green to A−, red to B+, blue to B−.

Coil Usual wire colours Terminals A black, green A+, A− B red, blue B+, B−

Not every maker follows it, so check with a multimeter on the resistance range: the two wires of one coil show the coil's resistance, a few ohms; two wires of different coils show no connection. Most datasheets also name the pairs (A/C and B/D, or the colours).

docs.title: Soldering
docs.text:
1. Cut the leads to a comfortable length: long enough to reach the pads with the board mounted, short enough not to get into the motor's shaft. If your firmware is older than 105 (see Releases and versions), leave them long enough to swap one pair later.
  2. Tin the leads and solder them to the pads: one coil to A+ and A−, the other to B+ and B−.
  3. Make sure no strand bridges two pads and that nothing touches the motor housing.

Check

With the driver unpowered, a multimeter shows the coil's resistance, a few ohms, between A+ and A− and between B+ and B−, and no strand bridges two pads.

Warning

Never connect or disconnect the motor while the driver is powered.

docs.title: Phase order and direction
docs.text:
Calibration spins the motor in open loop and watches the encoder.

With firmware 105 and newer, a reversed coil is detected and compensated in software (the firmware applies a reflection of the current frame, which is what a physical swap would do), so the motor calibrates identically with any wiring, and positive commands turn the motor counter-clockwise seen from the magnet side.

With firmware 103, a reversed coil fails the open-loop step with Open loop: Failed / Switch motor phases and try again!; swap A+ and A− and calibrate again.

Because calibration compensates the wiring, the positive direction is tied to the encoder: with firmware 105 and newer, swapping the wires of a coil and calibrating again does not change it.

The firmware has no setting that reverses it (#Dir is stored but not used). If you want the other direction to be positive, negate the setpoints and the position, speed and current you read back in your host program.

docs.title: First setup
docs.text:
From a mounted and wired driver to a calibrated, tuned motor. Motor GUI in the browser is the usual tool for it; every step also gives the terminal command, for a terminal or for the console in Motor GUI.

  1. Motor GUI: the browser, the serial adapter, opening the port, what is on the screen.
  2. The serial terminal: the alternative — PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor or the Arduino monitor, and the # commands.
  3. Motor parameters and calibration: the factory defaults, the motor's resistance, inductance and pole pairs, then the calibration run and what follows it.
  4. Encoder table and anti-cogging: the two corrections the driver measures on itself after a calibration, how to run them again and how to check them.
  5. Current limit and loop tuning: the current limit for the motor, the loop gains if the defaults do not suit it, the speed estimate and the delay compensation.
  6. Saving the configuration: nothing survives a power cycle until it is saved; where it is kept.

A driver that has been through these pages is ready for Operation. The Quick start is the same path in four short parts.

docs.title: Encoder table and anti-cogging
docs.text:
Firmware 109 measures two corrections on the drive itself, with nothing but the motor on the bench. The encoder table corrects the small error of the encoder's angle reading. The anti-cogging is a current that cancels the motor's own torque ripple.

After a calibration both run by themselves (What follows the calibration). This page explains what they are, how to run them again, and how to check them.

The motor turns

Each run turns the motor one revolution forward and one back, slowly. Keep the shaft free: nothing on it and nothing it could drive. A mechanism that cannot turn a whole revolution, a gripper's racks for example, has to come off first.

docs.title: The encoder table
docs.text:
The magnetic encoder reads the shaft angle with a small error that changes slowly around the turn. The magnet is never exactly on the axis, and the chip itself is not perfectly linear. On the bench NEMA 17 it was 0.61° peak to peak.

The commutation multiplies it by the pole pairs. On a 50-pole-pair stepper the field is then up to about 18 electrical degrees off at places: the 0.61° spans about 31° electrical, and the electrical offset sits near its middle. That costs torque and makes the current uneven around the turn.

To measure it, the driver turns the field open loop, one shaft revolution forward and one back at 2048 ticks/s (about 20 s). A current of 80 % of the current limit holds the rotor to the field.

At each 1/128 of a turn it records how far the encoder's angle is from the field's. Forward and backward are averaged, so friction, which pulls the rotor behind the field in each direction, cancels. The stepper's own pull towards its detents is left out by keeping only the harmonics 1 to 16 per turn.

Figure 5.6: Illustration, not a measurement: friction pulls the forward and the backward pass to either side of the encoder's error, and the detents add a fast ripple; their average, kept to the harmonics 1 to 16 per turn, is the table.

The result is a table of 128 corrections. From then on the encoder reading is corrected with it. The electrical offset is moved by the table's mean error, so the commutation stays right.

Figure 5.7: The encoder table of the bench NEMA 17: the encoder's error at each 1/128 of a turn, 0.61° peak to peak, about 31° electrical on the right-hand scale; the dashed line is its once-per-turn part.

A table over 4° peak to peak, or one that would move the offset by more than 60 electrical degrees, is rejected as implausible: the magnet is loose or far off its place.

docs.title: Anti-cogging
docs.text:
A stepper pulls towards its detent positions, four times per electrical turn. Errors in the current measurement add a ripple once and twice per electrical turn.

At low speed both show as a ripple in the speed and the position. Anti-cogging adds a current to the current setpoint that cancels it: a function of the electrical angle, added in velocity and position modes.

To find it, the driver runs in velocity mode at 1500 ticks/s (parameter 44), one motor revolution forward and one back. It records the current the velocity loop asks for in 256 bins over the electrical angle. Then it averages the two directions, each without its mean, so friction drops out.

From that it keeps two forms of the same correction:

  • harmonics (parameter 37 = 1): the 8 largest of the harmonics 1 to 32 of the electrical angle, each a·cos(h·θ) + b·sin(h·θ) in mA;
  • table (parameter 37 = 2): 256 values in mA over one electrical turn, interpolated between them.
Figure 5.8: The anti-cogging of the bench NEMA 17 over one electrical turn, identified at 1500 ticks/s before the drive had the encoder table and the zero trim: above, its two forms; below, the current the velocity loop asks for with it off and on.

The identification switches the harmonics on. On the bench both forms were equally good. Parameter 38 scales the correction from 0 to 200 % for experiments; 100 % is as identified.

The angle here comes from the encoder alone, without the calibration's offset. The part of the correction that comes from the current measurement is tied to the motor's electrical angle, though, which the offset defines. That is why #Calangle identifies the anti-cogging again.

The identification records the current the loops ask for, so it depends a little on the gains. After a large change of the current or velocity gains, identify it again.

docs.title: The current-sense zero trim
docs.text:
The once-per-electrical-turn part of the anti-cogging is mostly an error of the current-sense zero. On the bench it was 1.6 mA of ripple per ADC count of zero error.

The identification with the trim reads both zero errors from it and corrects the zeros. Then it identifies again on the corrected zeros.

Figure 5.9: The harmonics of the anti-cogging the drive identified on the bench NEMA 17, with the current-sense zeros as measured and with the zeros corrected by hand, as the trim corrects them: the 1st harmonic drops, the 2nd and 4th stay.

If the 1st harmonic did not drop by at least 30 % and is still above 2.0 mA, the zeros go back. The anti-cogging is then identified once more without the trim, and the state reads 11, done without the trim.

A 1st harmonic under 1.5 mA is left alone, and one run moves a zero by at most 30 counts.

The trims (parameters 59 and 60, up to ±60 counts) are saved with the encoder table. They are added to the zero the driver measures at every start-up. On the bench drive the trim took the 1st harmonic from 8.8 to 0.2 mA in one run. The plot above shows a correction by hand, 8.9 to 1.0 mA; the drive's own trim did better.

docs.title: Running them
docs.text:
The driver must be calibrated and without an error. Each run has a UART command and a CAN parameter:

What UART CAN: Send_Parameter the encoder table, used at once #Encal 52 = 1 the encoder table, used and saved #Encal save 52 = 2 the encoder table, then the anti-cogging with the trim, then save all #Encal all 52 = 3, or 43 = 3 the anti-cogging, switched on #Cogcal 43 = 1 the anti-cogging, switched on and saved #Cogcal save 43 = 2 the anti-cogging with the trim #Cogcal trim 43 = 4 the anti-cogging with the trim, saved #Par 43,5 43 = 5 stop a run #Encal stop, #Cogcal stop 52 = 0, 43 = 0

#Encal stop does not stop the anti-cogging part of a combined run (#Encal all). #Cogcal stop stops a run in either part, and so do 52 = 0 and 43 = 0 over CAN.

  1. Make sure the shaft is free: nothing on it and nothing it could drive.
  2. Send the run's command from the table, on the UART or over CAN.
  3. Send nothing else while the motor turns, one revolution forward and one back for each run.
  4. Read the result with #Encal state or #Cogcal state, or parameter 52 or 43 over CAN.

Check

The state reads 3, done, or 11, done without the trim. The motor holds the position the shaft reached. Any other state is in the table "When a run fails" under Checking them.

Both runs keep the CAN watchdog fed while they go, and end by holding the position the shaft reached. They stop at once when a host sends a command (a motion command, Idle) or an error comes up. Nothing is saved then.

While a run turns the motor a capture is not armed. During the anti-cogging run parameters 34 and 35 refuse a write: the runs use the capture's memory and the histogram.

A save from a run is the whole configuration, as #Save writes it. After a change of the motor, the magnet or its position, run the encoder table and the anti-cogging again, in that order, or calibrate again.

Two guards keep a correction from running on the wrong data:

  • parameter 37 refuses 1 or 2 while no set is stored for that form;
  • an encoder table measured on its own (52 = 1 or 2) switches an anti-cogging set from before off, because that set was found on the uncorrected encoder. The anti-cogging state then reads 10 until it is identified again.

docs.title: Checking them
docs.text:
#Info ends with what is in force:

In force:
  encoder table: on, error 0.61 deg p-p
  anti-cogging: on (harmonics), saved
  current-sense zero trim: -1 / 5 counts
  delay compensation: 166 us
  speed estimate: direct PLL, 60 Hz
  fast reading / fast PWM: on / on
  input filter: off; integral deadband: off
  after #Calangle (parameter 56): anti-cogging, then save

The example shows the values the bench drive measured. While a run goes, a line running: encoder table or running: anti-cogging identification follows.

#Encal state and #Cogcal state print one run's state without starting it. After a finished identification (state 3, or 11 without the trim) it also lists the harmonics.

Over CAN the same is in the parameters (the parameter table):

Parameter What it tells On the bench NEMA 17 52 the encoder table's state: 3 done, 4 aborted, 5 error or not calibrated, 6 the rotor did not follow, 7 rejected 3 54 the table's error peak to peak, 0.01° of the shaft 61-65 (0.61-0.65°); two runs within 0.021° 55 the amplitude of its once-per-turn part, 0.01° of the shaft 19 (0.19°) 57 how far the last table moved the electrical offset, 0.1° electrical −25, then −1 on a second run 43 the anti-cogging state: 3 done, 11 done without the trim, 6 the shaft did not turn 3 45 the cogging current found, 0.1 mA rms 71 (7.1 mA) 62, 63 the 1st harmonic before and after the trim, 0.1 mA 88, then 2 59, 60 the zero trims, counts −1, 5 79 the bits of what is in force, see What is in force

With the anti-cogging on, the bench motor's speed ripple that repeats with the angle was 1.2 to 2 times smaller at 1500 to 6000 ticks/s. The position ripple was 1.9 to 2.5 times smaller.

Figure 5.10: The speed of the bench NEMA 17 turning at 6000 ticks/s, minus its mean, before the drive had the encoder table and the zero trim: with the anti-cogging on, the part that repeats with the angle is about half as large.

A free motor gains little from the encoder table in these numbers. Its current varied 2.5 to 3 times less around the turn, but a free motor needs little current. A loaded one gains more.

Send_Buffer_Read reads the corrections themselves: kind 4 the encoder table (128 values in 1/16 count), kind 2 the harmonics, kind 3 the anti-cogging table (Respond_Buffer_Data).

When a run fails:

State Cause What to do 52 = 6, 43 = 6 the rotor did not follow: the shaft is blocked, or the current is too low to turn it free the shaft; for the encoder table raise the current limit (it uses 80 % of it) 52 = 5, 43 = 5 the driver was in error or is not calibrated #Error, clear it, calibrate 52 = 4, 43 = 4 a command came first run it again and send nothing meanwhile 52 = 7 the table is implausible check the magnet: glued, centred, at the right distance (The encoder magnet), then calibrate 43 = 8 the encoder table of a combined run failed parameter 52 says why

docs.title: Switching them off
docs.text:
UART CAN: Send_Parameter the encoder table off / on #Encal off, #Encal on 53 = 0, 53 = 1 the anti-cogging off, harmonics, table #Par 37,0, #Par 37,1, #Par 37,2 37 = 0, 1, 2 how much of the anti-cogging #Par 38, and the percentage 38 = 0 to 200 (%)

#Save keeps the switches with the corrections. #Default clears both corrections and the trims.

Spectral Micro

The Spectral Micro firmware 109 has the same encoder table and anti-cogging. It runs neither after a calibration until they are tested on its bench, and it skips the zero trim. Its manual says more.

docs.title: Motor parameters and calibration
docs.text:
Calibration teaches the driver its motor. It:

  • checks the magnet and the supply;
  • takes the motor's resistance, inductance and pole pairs from you;
  • computes the current loop gains;
  • spins the motor in open loop to learn the direction of the wiring;
  • finds the angle offset between the encoder and the motor's electrical zero;
  • measures the motor constants Kt, KV and the flux linkage.

From firmware 109 two more runs follow by themselves, the encoder table and the anti-cogging, and then the driver saves everything. It runs once per motor; the result is kept by saving.

The motor turns

Calibration spins the motor in both directions, fast at times. Fix the motor to the bench and take everything off the shaft.

Supply voltage

Calibrate at 24 V. From firmware 109 KV and Kt no longer depend on the supply or on #Vlim: the spins that measure them run at their own 6 V limit, and yours is put back afterwards.

docs.title: 1. Restore the defaults
docs.text:
The EEPROM of a new driver, or of one that ran another motor, can hold values that do not fit, such as another motor's parameters. Calibration starts from what is there, so start from the factory values.

(A damaged configuration should not show up with firmware 106 and newer, which checks the stored blocks at power-up and replaces a damaged one with the defaults; if #Info still shows -1 somewhere, restoring the defaults fixes it.)

Motor GUITerminal

Default in the settings.

#Default

This also resets the serial number, hardware version and batch date stored in the EEPROM, and clears an encoder table and an anti-cogging set from another motor; note the hardware version and batch date #Info prints if you need them. From firmware 109 the CAN node ID is kept. Saving the configuration says what else it does.

docs.title: 2. Enter the motor parameters
docs.text:
STEPFOC does not measure the resistance and inductance of a stepper (the Spectral Micro does for a BLDC); you enter them from the motor's datasheet, as the values of one coil, and the pole pairs. Calibration fails on a value left at 0, and accepts only 50, 75, 100 or 125 pole pairs.

We recommend a Motor GUI preset

In Motor GUI's Presets tab, a preset enters these values for you, with safe limits and gains. For a Source Robotics product, pick its preset. For any other stepper, pick Generic motor and type the pole pairs, the resistance and the inductance from the datasheet: the preset writes them with a low current limit and soft loops, so the motor calibrates safely. More: Motor GUI.

Motor GUITerminalCAN

In the motor settings enter Pole pairs (50 for a 1.8° motor, 75 for 1.2°, 100 for 0.9°, 125 for 0.72°), Resistance in ohms and Inductance in henries, and apply them.

#PP 50          1.8° stepper: 50; 1.2°: 75; 0.9°: 100; 0.72°: 125
#R 1.1          phase resistance in ohms
#L 0.0026       phase inductance in henries (2.6 mH)

Parameters 78 (pole pairs), 76 (resistance in mΩ) and 77 (inductance in µH) hold the same values, for a host that sets a drive up over the bus: Send_Parameter(78, 50), Send_Parameter(76, 1100), Send_Parameter(77, 2600). The calibration itself runs over the serial port.

Figure 5.5: The three values on a typical datasheet, here for the 17HS16-2004S1: 1.8°, 1.1 Ω, 2.6 mH.

Calibration computes the current loop gains from R, L and the current loop bandwidth, 160 Hz by default: Kp = ω·L and Ki = ω·R, with ω = 2π × the bandwidth.

The firmware keeps Ki per control loop, so Ki_iq in the log is about ω·R × 160 µs. Leave the bandwidth for now; Current limit and loop tuning comes back to it. (Firmware 108 and older divided both gains by 7, which gave a loop of about 70 Hz.)

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal

Start the calibration. The driver enters Calibration mode and the GUI shows its log step by step; when it finishes, the phase order and direction, Kt, KV and the flux linkage it found appear in the settings.

#Cal

The LED flashes fast while the routine runs, and the driver prints each step as it goes:

----------------
Calibration mode
----------------
Pole pair test: Passed
Magnet test: Passed
Vbus test: Passed
Resistance = 1.100000Ohm
Inductance = 0.002600H
Kp_iq = ...
Ki_iq = ...
Open loop direction: good
Calibrating angle offset... stage 1/13, sweep point 0
...
Angle offset is: ...
Alignment check: ... ticks/s, flipped ..., offsets ... / ...
Phase order is good!
KV is: ...
Kt is: ...
KV runs: ... ... ... ... (same direction within ... %)
Flux linkage is: ...
----------------
Calibration success!
Next, by itself: the encoder table, then anti-cogging (about a minute; keep the shaft free). Everything is saved when they finish (#Encal state, #Cogcal state)
Going to idle!
----------------

#Calonly runs the same calibration and nothing after it; it ends with Save config with #Save instead.

What the steps are:

Step What happens Fails with Pole pair test the entered pole pairs are one of 50, 75, 100, 125 Pole pair test: Failed and the list of values Magnet test the encoder sees enough field: a magnet is there and close enough. The test says nothing about centring, the gap or the glue Magnet test: Failed: magnet missing, too far, or axially magnetised Vbus test the supply is within limits Vbus test: Failed Resistance, inductance the entered values are not 0; they are printed back and Kp_iq, Ki_iq computed from them and the bandwidth Resistance test: Failed / Inductance test: Failed, with Please enter your stepper resistance by using #R command Open loop the motor is stepped open loop at a fixed 5000 mV. The direction the encoder saw is remembered, so a reversed coil is compensated from here on nothing in this firmware: the step always reports good, and a motor that did not turn fails the next step Angle offset a short spin checks that the motor turns (two tries, 90 electrical degrees apart); then the field locks the rotor and a sweep finds the offset at which both directions turn alike. It prints Calibrating angle offset... with its progress every half second Phase order is wrong! / Switch motor phases and try again!: the motor did not turn on either try. A line Spin-confirm delta: … ticks (need > 8192), Vbus: … mV says how far it turned and at what voltage. When the lock or the check after it fails instead, Angle alignment gave up: names the reason (it timed out, the rotor did not turn under current or the rotor turned the wrong way, also after flipping), followed by Check speed … ticks/s (need > 1000), flipped …, offsets … rad and Try again; if it repeats, check the motor, its wiring and that the shaft is free Kt, KV, flux linkage four spins from standstill at 500 mA, about a second each and alternately forward and back, at a 6 V limit; KV is the mean speed per volt, Kt follows as 8.27 ÷ KV and the flux linkage from Kt. KV runs: in the log shows all four and how far they agree nothing: KV runs differ by more than 5 %: calibrate again, and check that the shaft is free is a warning, and the calibration still succeeds

A whole run takes up to about a minute, most of it in the angle-offset search. When a step fails, the log ends with Calibration failed!, the driver goes to idle, the motor counts as not calibrated and the LED stays on steadily. Nothing is saved; fix the cause and run #Cal again.

The 'Switch motor phases' message

It is left over from firmware 103, which needed the coils wired a particular way. Since firmware 105 the wiring is detected and compensated, so Phase order is wrong! / Switch motor phases and try again! means the motor did not turn or did not respond: a coil not connected or shorted, a supply too weak, or a magnet that slips. Swapping wires does not fix it. (Open loop: Failed with the same advice cannot appear in this release.)

The measured values are estimates

KV, Kt and the flux linkage come from one short spin and differ a little from one run to the next, more on motors with uneven windings. For the loops this does not matter; for a torque estimate in newton-metres, measure Kt yourself.

docs.title: What follows the calibration
docs.text:
Half a second after Calibration success! of a #Cal the driver starts two runs on its own: the encoder table (about 20 s), then the anti-cogging identification with the current-sense zero trim (about 25 to 70 s). When they succeed, everything is saved.

The motor turns slowly, one turn forward and one back for each run, so keep the shaft free for about a minute more; #Info shows running: … under In force: while they go.

A command from a host (a motion command, #Idle) stops them; then nothing is saved, and the calibration is kept only if you #Save it. Encoder table and anti-cogging explains both and how to check them. #Cal always runs them; #Calonly never does.

Set the current limit before you calibrate

The encoder table turns the field with a current of 80 % of the current limit, for about 20 s. Calibration uses its own 1600 mA for its steps and puts the limit that was in force back when it ends, before the encoder table runs; after #Default that is 1700 mA, about 1.4 A in the coils, more than a small motor is rated for. So set #Ilim for the motor before #Cal (a Motor GUI preset does; known issue KI-19).

Not yet tested on the bench

The runs after a calibration and #Calonly were tested on the bench on 2026-11-10 (#Calonly 25 times on a 20 mm motor, #Cal with both runs on a 40 mm and a 60 mm motor). Parameters 76 to 79 and #Par came last in firmware 109 and had not been tested on the bench when this page was written.

docs.title: 4. Save
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal

Save. The GUI marks Unsaved changes until you do.

#Save

After #Cal the driver saves by itself when the runs succeed; save anyway once they are done, or after #Calonly. Without a save the calibration is gone at the next power cycle. The driver goes to idle and the LED shows normal operation; the state shows Calibrated and the constants.

The current limit

Calibration uses its own 1600 mA for its steps. From firmware 109 it puts the limit that was in force back when it ends, so a save stores your limit; firmware 108 and older left 1600 mA in force (known issue KI-2). If the limit is still the 1700 mA of #Default, set it for your motor with #Ilim and save again (Current limit and loop tuning).

Check

After a power cycle #Info prints Calibrated and the constants calibration found, and Motor GUI shows Calibrated. Not calibrated means the save did not happen: calibrate and save again.

docs.title: When to calibrate again
docs.text:
• After changing the motor, the magnet or the wiring.
  • After restoring the defaults.
  • After a firmware update that clears the calibration (a release note says so when it does).

A calibration that reports success but a motor that runs badly afterwards usually means the magnet moved on the shaft between calibration and use: fix the magnet and calibrate again.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Message Cause Magnet test: Failed no magnet, magnet too far (more than about 1.5 mm), or an axially magnetised magnet Vbus test: Failed supply off, too low, or the cable the wrong way round (if the driver survived it) Resistance test: Failed, Inductance test: Failed the resistance or the inductance still 0 Phase order is wrong! see the note above: the motor did not turn on the spin check; check the four wires and their solder joints, the supply and its current limit, and the magnet Angle alignment gave up: after Phase order is wrong! the lock or the check after it failed, and the line names the reason; run #Cal again, and if it repeats check the motor, its wiring and that the shaft is free Cal: not started, the E-stop is latched (#Clear first), or Stopped by an E-stop: #Clear, then calibrate again. after Calibration failed! an E-stop is latched or ended the calibration: #Clear, then #Cal; the alignment starts again from its first stage the routine stops in a step and prints nothing more reset the driver (#Reset) and try again; the angle-offset search prints a progress line every half second, so wait for a minute before you decide success, but the LED stays on and no error is reported should not happen with firmware 106 and newer, which replaces a damaged configuration block with the defaults at power-up. If #Info shows -1 somewhere, restore the defaults, enter the parameters and calibrate again

#Calangle runs an angle-offset search on its own, with an older routine than the one #Cal uses: it gives up after about two minutes and keeps the offset it reached. From firmware 109, when parameter 56 is not 0, the anti-cogging is identified again afterwards and everything is saved, because the anti-cogging depends on the offset.

After a timeout nothing follows and nothing is saved. From firmware 109 #Calangle is refused while the driver is in error: it prints Calangle: not started, the drive is in error (#Error, #Clear). After a change of motor, magnet or wiring, run the whole #Cal instead.

Calibration runs over the serial connection only: a terminal, or Motor GUI over the serial adapter, not over CAN.

docs.title: Motor GUI
docs.text: Motor GUI is the usual way to set up, test and tune a driver: a tool in the browser that connects to one driver over the serial adapter or to a bus of drivers over the CANvas adapter, shows the state, moves the motor, runs the calibration, tunes the loops with live plots, records telemetry and updates the firmware. Nothing is installed. Everything it does, the driver also does from a terminal or from Python — the GUI reads and writes the same settings — so every procedure in this manual shows the GUI first and the terminal command beside it.

docs.title: The browser
docs.text: Motor GUI reaches the hardware through the browser's serial port access (Web Serial), which Chromium-based browsers have: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera. Firefox and Safari cannot open serial ports.

docs.title: Two ways to connect
docs.text: Adapter Use it for One driver over serial the 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter on the driver's UART connector, 256000 baud the first setup and calibration (calibration runs over UART only), tuning on the bench A bus over CAN the CANvas adapter; it appears as a serial port and speaks slcan every driver on the bus by its node ID: testing a machine, updating firmware on all joints

docs.title: Opening the port
docs.text:
1. Plug in the adapter and the motor supply. The adapter alone powers the driver's logic, enough to open the port and read the settings, but the driver reports a Vbus error and will not calibrate or move until the supply is on.
  2. Open motorgui.com, choose the connection kind, and Connect. The browser asks which port; pick the adapter's.
  3. The driver's identity appears: hardware version, firmware version, serial number, batch date, whether it is calibrated and activated, and the active errors: what #Info, #SERNUM and #Error print in a terminal.

If the port is not offered, the browser is not Chromium-based, or another program holds the port (a terminal left open, PlatformIO's monitor), or the operating system does not give the browser the port:

WindowsLinuxmacOS

The adapter is COM and a number. Device Manager lists it under Ports (COM & LPT): the entry that disappears when you unplug the adapter is yours. An adapter that shows a warning sign there instead needs the driver of its USB chip (on most 3.3 V adapters a CP210x or a CH340) from the chip maker.

The serial adapter is /dev/ttyUSB0 on most adapters, the CANvas adapter /dev/ttyACM0; ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM* lists them. To open them without root, join the dialout group once, then log out and in again:

sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER

The serial adapter is /dev/cu.usbserial- and a few characters on most adapters, the CANvas adapter /dev/cu.usbmodem and a number; ls /dev/cu.* lists them. Use the cu. name, not the tty. one, in a terminal or a script.

The browser's port picker lists the same adapters. If the port opens and nothing appears: the driver is unpowered, or TX and RX are crossed on an adapter that is not the Source Robotics one.

docs.title: What is on the screen
docs.text:
• State: the identity above, the control mode the driver is in, the errors, and Clear errors.
  • Jog: Jog position, Jog velocity and Jog current move the motor in the matching control mode; Send setpoint sends a value in the current mode. Live stream while dragging follows a slider as you move it.
  • Plots of position, speed and current, panning and zooming, with the value under the pointer.
  • Settings: the motor parameters (pole pairs, resistance, inductance), the limits (current, velocity, voltage), the loop gains with Apply gains and Apply preset, the CAN node ID, the watchdog, the thermistor. The GUI marks Unsaved changes until you Save to the driver's EEPROM; Default restores the factory values.
  • Calibration: starts #Cal and shows the driver's log step by step; afterwards the phase order and direction, Kt, KV and the flux linkage it found.
  • Telemetry: the stream from the driver, and recordings of it for a test or a bug report.
  • Firmware update: the releases from GitHub, flashed through the bootloader; Scan bootloaders on a bus.
  • Gripper: the gripper controls, for a driver in gripper mode.
  • Console: type any # command by hand; the answer appears below it.
  • Wiring diagrams and Keyboard shortcuts under help.

docs.title: Screen guide
docs.text:
1 2 3

Figure 5.1: 1. Transport: choose UART for the serial adapter. 2. Baud: 256000 for a stock driver. 3. Connect: choose the adapter in the browser's port picker.

1 2 3 4

Figure 5.2: 1. Connection and node: confirm the intended driver. 2. State: calibration, activation and faults. 3. Command mode: setpoints and jog controls. 4. Live telemetry: measured position, speed and current. This screenshot uses Mock CAN (demo), not physical hardware.

Check

After connecting real hardware, the state and identity belong to your driver. If they do not appear, check the transport, the selected port, the supply and the TX/RX wiring before trying to move.

docs.title: Try it without hardware
docs.text: Open Motor GUI, choose Mock CAN (demo), and press Connect. The motor and gripper panels run in the browser without a port picker. Motor calibration (#Cal) still requires a real UART connection; the CAN demo does not perform it.

docs.title: What next
docs.text: Motor parameters and calibration is the first thing to do with a connected driver; Working in Motor GUI covers everyday use: moving the motor, the plots, recordings, several motors on a bus.

docs.title: Saving the configuration
docs.text:
Nothing you set survives a power cycle until you save it.

Motor GUITerminal

Save. The GUI marks Unsaved changes until you do.

#Save

Saving writes the configuration to the EEPROM: the motor parameters and the calibration, every gain and limit, the CAN node ID (and the bootloader's board ID with it), the heartbeat and watchdog settings, the thermistor and LED settings and the gripper flag.

From firmware 109 also the tool id and the watchdog fallback, the anti-cogging set with its mode and scale, and the encoder table with its on/off switch, parameter 56 and the current-sense zero trims.

Over CAN, Send_Save_config does the same. Save after calibration, after tuning, and after changing the node ID. The runs after a calibration save by themselves when they succeed.

Some settings are not kept and start from their defaults at every power-up:

  • the current loop bandwidth (#Cbw, 160 Hz; the gains it computed are kept);
  • the idle behaviour (#Brake / #Coast or Send_Settings: brake);
  • the open-loop and calibration settings (#Openv, #Opens, #Vp, #Iqoffset, #microstep, #stepinterval);
  • the parameters of firmware 109 that tune the loops: the speed estimate (direct PLL at 60 Hz), the commutation delay compensation (166 µs), the fast reading and PWM paths (on), the sin/cos table (off), the position input filter and the velocity-integral deadband (off), the anti-cogging identification speed, the d-axis current, and the capture and histogram settings.

The Defaults reference marks each setting, and the parameter table says for every parameter whether it is kept.

A saved watchdog runs from power-up

With a watchdog saved (Send_Watchdog), the driver starts its count at power-up. A host that sends no motion frame or status request within the watchdog time finds the driver in watchdog error, and clears it with Send_Clear_Error. See Over CAN.

The serial number

This firmware does not read the serial number back from the EEPROM at power-up: #SERNUM reports 1 until it is set, and every save writes the value held in RAM over the stored one.

docs.title: The defaults
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal

Default in the settings.

#Default

Restoring the defaults writes the factory values to the EEPROM and reloads them. It also sets the thermistor to off, resets the serial number, the hardware version and the batch date stored in the EEPROM, and clears the gripper flag, the heartbeat rate and the watchdog.

From firmware 109 it also clears the tool id, the watchdog fallback, the anti-cogging set, the encoder table and its zero trims, and sets parameter 56 back to its default.

The CAN node ID is kept from firmware 109 (it is 0 only when no valid ID is stored); firmware 108 and older set it to 0. Note the hardware version and batch date #Info prints before you use it. The defaults are listed in the Defaults reference.

Use it before the first calibration of a motor, after a firmware update when the driver behaves oddly, and when the state shows nonsense values (a -1 where a number should be). With firmware 106 and newer that should not happen: the driver checks the stored configuration at power-up and replaces a damaged block with the defaults by itself.

docs.title: Where it is kept: the EEPROM
docs.text:
The configuration lives in an EEPROM chip on the board (a 24C16, 2 KB), apart from the firmware: flashing a new firmware never touches it, and only the firmware's check at power-up decides to reset a part of it. Since firmware 106 the configuration is in blocks, each with its own checksum; firmware 109 adds three:

Block Bytes Checksum at Holds calibration 60-188, reserved 212-236 208 pole pairs, R, L, Kt, KV, flux linkage, angle offset, phase order, commutation direction, the current gains settings 1 44-180 192 CAN ID, limits, the other gains, watchdog, heartbeat, thermistor, LED, gripper flag settings 2 (109) 260-312 256 tool id, watchdog fallback, the product stamp, the calibration ID; reserved slots anti-cogging (109) 324-879 320 the harmonics, the table, mode and scale encoder table (109) 884-1147 880 the table, its on/off switch, parameter 56, the current-sense zero trims
