At power-up a block whose checksum does not match is read again, up to three times. If it still does not match, it gets its defaults, alone, and the others stay; a settings reset keeps a valid CAN ID.

A board saved by firmware 101 to 105, from before the checksums, is trusted when the first 109 start finds anything it ever saved, and sealed with checksums then.

The new blocks need the chip's upper banks; on a smaller chip they keep their defaults in RAM and are not saved, which #Info says (Settings block 2: not available, block 3 not available) and the identity frame's flag bit 3 shows.

Going back to an older firmware is safe: the first two blocks are unchanged, and older firmware ignores everything from byte 256 on. Upgrading from older firmware says what changes when you update.

docs.title: What the driver reports
docs.text:
The state Motor GUI shows is what is in the EEPROM and what the driver measures. In a terminal it takes three commands:

  • #Info prints the hardware and firmware version, the CAN ID, the calibration state and the motor parameters (pole pairs, resistance, inductance, Kt and KV), and from firmware 109 the build, the board ID and the calibration ID, the tool id, the watchdog, the EEPROM blocks and, at its end, what is in force;
  • #Param prints the gains and limits;
  • #Error the active errors.

They are the first thing to look at when something is off, and the thing to copy into a bug report. Status and diagnostics explains the new lines.

docs.title: The serial terminal
docs.text:
Motor GUI is the usual way to work with the driver; a plain serial terminal is the alternative, and it is what the console inside Motor GUI is.

Everything in this manual that is done in the GUI is also one # command, and the terminal shows the driver's answers exactly as it prints them, which is useful when something does not work.

The driver talks on its UART connector at 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V. Any terminal that sends a line ending in CR+LF works.

Figure 5.3: The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
1. Plug the USB-to-serial adapter into the UART connector with the UART cable. With another adapter: 3.3 V only, and cross TX and RX: the driver's TX to the adapter's RX, the driver's RX to the adapter's TX.
  2. Connect the motor supply. The adapter's 3.3 V powers the driver's logic, so the driver answers over UART with only the adapter plugged in, but it reports a Vbus error and refuses calibration and every motion command until the 12 to 29 V supply is on.
  3. Find the adapter's port:
WindowsLinuxmacOS

The adapter is COM and a number. Device Manager lists it under Ports (COM & LPT): the entry that disappears when you unplug the adapter is yours. An adapter that shows a warning sign there instead needs the driver of its USB chip (on most 3.3 V adapters a CP210x or a CH340) from the chip maker.

The serial adapter is /dev/ttyUSB0 on most adapters, the CANvas adapter /dev/ttyACM0; ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM* lists them. To open them without root, join the dialout group once, then log out and in again:

sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER

The serial adapter is /dev/cu.usbserial- and a few characters on most adapters, the CANvas adapter /dev/cu.usbmodem and a number; ls /dev/cu.* lists them. Use the cu. name, not the tty. one, in a terminal or a script.

Danger

5 V on the UART pins destroys the board.

docs.title: A terminal
docs.text:
PuTTYVS Code (PlatformIO)Arduino IDE

PuTTY needs to send CR+LF when you press Enter, which the stock build cannot. Use the modified PuTTY: under Terminal → Keyboard select the CR LF option, then open the serial port at 256000.

Keyboard setting Session

With the firmware project open in VS Code with the PlatformIO extension, the serial monitor (the plug icon in the status bar) uses the speed and the send_on_enter filter from platformio.ini, so a line goes out with CR+LF when you press Enter.

platformio.ini The monitor

Select the adapter's port under Tools, any board (the monitor does not care), open the serial monitor, set 256000 baud and Both NL & CR as the line ending.

Figure 5.4: The Arduino serial monitor at 256000 baud, with Both NL & CR as the line ending.

docs.title: The first commands
docs.text:
#Info

prints the driver's identity and state: the hardware and firmware version, the CAN ID, the calibration state and the motor parameters. #Help (firmware 106 and newer) prints a short command reference, #Error the active errors, #Param the gains and limits.

Check

#Info answers with the driver's identity, the hardware and firmware version first. If nothing comes back: the baud rate, the CR+LF line ending, TX and RX, see The driver does not answer.

Every command starts with #, and a Set/Get command takes one number after a space: #P 16384 moves to position 16384; #P alone prints the position. Names are case-sensitive. The whole set is in the UART commands reference, and Over UART explains the protocol.

docs.title: Current limit and loop tuning
docs.text:
Calibration leaves the driver with current loop gains computed for your motor and with velocity and position gains that suit a bare stepper.

Two things remain: the current limit, which you must set for your motor, and the loop gains, which you tune if the defaults do not suit it. Motor GUI shows the motor's response on its plots while you change a gain, which is what makes tuning quick.

docs.title: The current limit
docs.text:
Set the current limit to the rated phase current of your motor in mA (the datasheet value; the tested motors' ratings are in Tested motors).

It is 1700 mA after #Default; calibration uses its own 1600 mA for its steps and, from firmware 109, puts your limit back when it ends. Set it before you calibrate: the encoder table that follows a calibration runs at 80 % of it.

#Ilim clamps the limit to the driver's 2800 mA and takes the magnitude of a negative number. The firmware does not trip on phase current by itself and does not monitor the driver stage. A limit above the motor's rating overheats the motor.

Over CAN

From firmware 109 Send_Limits stops the current limit at 2800 mA, as #Ilim does, and ignores a negative value. Firmware 108 and older stored it as sent (known issue KI-1). A host program must still keep it within the motor's rating.

Motor GUITerminal

In the limits set the current limit, then Save.

#Ilim 1500
#Save

Crunching and whining sounds at speed usually mean the current limit, or the current loop gains, are too high.

docs.title: The loops
docs.text:
Figure 5.11: The position loop commands the velocity loop, which commands the current loop.

Tune from the inside out: the current loop first, then velocity, then position. Before you start:

  • The motor must be calibrated and without active errors; the driver refuses the control modes otherwise.
  • Fix the motor to the bench, nothing on the shaft. A loop that oscillates can shake a loose motor off the table.
  • If the defaults oscillate, lower all gains until the motor is quiet, then raise them one at a time in small steps.
Motor GUITerminal

The gains are in the settings: change one, Apply gains, command a move with the jog controls and read the response on the plots. Apply preset loads a starting set for a kind of motor: a product preset writes its own current and velocity gains; the Generic motor presets set soft limits and velocity gains and leave the current gains to #Cbw and the calibration. Apply a preset before you calibrate, so that the calibration computes the current gains, and set the velocity gains after it. Save when you are done.

Each gain is a command: #Kpiq 0.5, #Kpv 0.02, …, then #Save. Command a move with #Iq, #V or #P and judge the response by ear and by #Cyc 20, which streams position, speed and current.

docs.title: The current loop
docs.text:
The current loop is a PI controller that turns a current request into a voltage. Its gains Kpiq and Kiiq follow from the motor's resistance R, its inductance L and one number, the bandwidth: Kp = ω·L and Ki = ω·R, with ω = 2π × the bandwidth.

The firmware keeps Ki per control loop: Kiiq is about ω·R × 160 µs. For 1.1 Ω, 2.6 mH and 160 Hz that gives Kpiq 2.70 and Kiiq 0.177.

Do not enter ω·R as #Kiiq. The PI then cancels the coil's own lag, and the current follows a request like a first-order filter at that bandwidth. Calibration computes them this way at 160 Hz, the default; so does setting the bandwidth:

TerminalCAN 
#Cbw 200          new gains at once from R and L; it prints them
#Save             keeps the gains (the bandwidth itself is 160 again after a power cycle)

Send_Parameter(49, 200), then Send_Save_config. Reading parameter 49 gives the bandwidth the gains in force amount to with the R and L in force.

The bandwidth can be 10 to 625 Hz (a tenth of the 6250 Hz control loop). A higher one follows a request and rejects a disturbance faster, and is louder; on the bench, 160 Hz followed an injected ripple better than the old gains and stayed stable.

Gains set by hand with #Kpiq and #Kiiq work too; parameter 49 then tells which bandwidth they amount to.

Drives calibrated with older firmware

Firmware 108 and older divided both gains by 7, a loop of about 70 Hz. Their saved gains stay as they are after an update to 109: parameter 49 reads about 71 Hz until the drive is calibrated again, or #Cbw 160 and #Save are sent. See Upgrading from older firmware.

Test with a current setpoint of a few hundred mA (Jog current, or #Iq 300): the motor should push with a steady, quiet torque. Keep the current well under the limit.

docs.title: The velocity loop
docs.text:
The firmware's start values are Kpv 0.02 and Kiv 0.001, tuned on the bench with a bare NEMA 17 and the speed estimate below: it vibrated at Kpv 0.056, and 0.02 is about half of that; Kiv rang at 0.004, and 0.001 halved the speed ripple at 300 to 1500 ticks/s. #Default and a settings reset write the same values.

A drive saved with older firmware keeps its saved gains after an update (typically 0.007 and 0.0005): set #Kpv 0.02 and #Kiv 0.001 and #Save (a 21.5 mm stepper overshot 95 % at these on the bench; its presets use #Kpv 0.014 and #Kiv 0.00014). To tune for your motor and load:

  1. Raise Kpv until the motor vibrates at a steady speed command, then take about half of it.
  2. Raise Kiv slowly until the speed rings after a change, then back off well below that. Kiv is an integrator: too much makes the motor unstable, none leaves a steady-state error.
  3. Test with a speed setpoint (Jog velocity, or #V 20000; 16384 ticks per second is one revolution per second) and with different speeds.

A motor geared into a joint carries more inertia than a bare one and usually takes other gains; tune it in place.

docs.title: The position loop
docs.text:
1. Raise Kpp until the motor overshoots or oscillates when it reaches a target, then back off.
  2. Test with a position step (Jog position, or #P 16384 and #P 0): one revolution and back. The response should be quick, without overshoot; the plot shows both.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Run the motor over the whole range of speeds and loads it will see, with a load if you can, and adjust. Then save.

docs.title: The speed estimate
docs.text:
The velocity loop needs the speed, which the driver estimates from the encoder count. Parameter 50 picks how:

Parameter 50 Estimate How it behaves 0 moving average of the last 20 count differences about 1.5 ms late, in steps of 312 ticks/s: the old estimate 1 PLL, the speed is its integrator smooth, a little late 2 (default) direct PLL, integrator plus the proportional term almost no lag, a little more noise

Both PLLs are critically damped at the natural frequency of parameter 51, 60 Hz by default (10 to 312 Hz).

The lag of the moving average was what limited the velocity gain: on the bench the direct PLL at 60 Hz allowed 40 % more Kpv before the motor vibrated, and the speed ripple was 23 to 50 % lower at 1500 to 24000 ticks/s; its extra noise did not reach the current.

Calibration and the gripper's stop detection always use the moving average, which they were tuned with. Both parameters are not kept by Save: every power-up starts with the direct PLL at 60 Hz. The speed in Respond_data_pack_1 and Send_Respond_Encoder_data, the watchdog descend and the capture is the picked estimate.

docs.title: Commutation delay compensation
docs.text:
The voltage a control loop sets reaches the motor later than the angle it was computed from was read: the rest of the loop, the wait for the PWM update and half a control period.

By then the rotor has turned on, and the voltage lands a little behind the angle it was meant for. Parameter 64 turns the output voltage forward by the angle the rotor covers in that delay, in the closed-loop modes above 100 ticks/s.

166 µs is the default, measured on the bench drive: the d-axis voltage against the cross-coupling the motor's inductance makes, at 12000 to 48000 ticks/s, fitted over 15 points. 0 switches it off; 1 to 500 µs are accepted. It is not kept by Save, so 166 µs is in force after every power-up.

docs.title: The finer points of the velocity loop
docs.text:
Two settings for special cases, both off by default and not kept by Save:

  • Position input filter, parameter 74 (Hz, 0 to 250). A host that sends positions at a fixed rate sends a staircase; without the speed the steps are all the loops see. The filter turns the staircase into a smooth path and makes its own speed from it, in position and PD modes. Use it only for a host that sends positions without the speed feedforward, at about the host's rate ÷ 12 (8 Hz for 100 Hz). On the bench it cut the tracking error of such a host from 1023 to 260 ticks at 12 Hz; with a host that sends the speed it made the tracking worse, so leave it off then.
  • Velocity-integral deadband, parameter 75 (ticks, 0 to 2000). In position mode the velocity integral sees the position error less this band, so a holding motor stops pushing against a small error it cannot correct. It trades accuracy for holding current: on the bench 5 ticks took the holding current from 16 to 3.4 mA, and the mean error grew from 1.5 to 6.4 ticks.

docs.title: Impedance (PD) mode
docs.text:
Figure 5.12: The impedance loop: a spring (KP) and a damper (KD) around the position setpoint, plus a current feedforward.

In PD mode the motor behaves like a spring and a damper: the current setpoint is KP × (setpoint − position) + KD × (speed setpoint − speed) + feedforward current, in mA, with the position in ticks and the speed in ticks/s. So KP is in mA per tick and KD in mA per tick/s.

Set KP and KD (the gains, or #KP, #KD, or Send_PD_Gains), then command with #PD, #PDV and #PDI or Send_data_pack_PD. Start with a small KP and KD of 0, raise KP until the motor holds position firmly, then add KD until it stops ringing. The theory corner explains the loop.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The velocity limit (#Vlimit, 800000 by default) clamps the speed the loops may command, in encoder ticks per second. A rough maximum for your motor is 0.8 × V × KV × 16384 / 60 ticks per second, with KV from calibration and V the lower of the voltage limit and the supply voltage.
  • The voltage limit (#Vlim) clamps the voltage of the current loops in mV. It is 6000 mV by default: a stepper's low resistance makes the current loop unstable with the full supply voltage, and the firmware's own guidance is 6000 mV for a phase resistance below 2 Ω. The limit also caps the top speed. 0, or a value above the supply voltage, uses the supply voltage.
  • #Rstint 1 resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which avoids windup when a program sends one setpoint after another with large steps.

docs.title: Operation
docs.text: How a calibrated driver is used: the control modes and what each one does, the two ways to talk to the driver and the two tools on top of them, what happens when something goes wrong, and gripper mode.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Control modes
  • Over UART
  • Over CAN
  • The watchdog: what the driver does when the host stops talking
  • With Python
  • Working in Motor GUI
  • Errors and recovery
  • Sound: tones, tunes and recorded sound through the motor
  • Status and diagnostics: what is in force, the identity, telemetry, the loop time, captures
  • Gripper mode

The exact layout of every message and command is in the API reference.

docs.title: Over CAN
docs.text:
CAN is the interface for running a machine: compact frames, a fixed cost per message, up to 14 drivers on one bus, and a host that can be a PC, a microcontroller or a robot control box.

The driver answers a motion command with its position, speed and current in the same frame exchange, so a control loop on the host needs one frame out and one frame back per motor and cycle.

docs.title: The frame
docs.text:
CAN 2.0 data frames with 11-bit identifiers at 1 Mbit/s. The identifier carries the node, the command and the error state:

Figure 6.2: Bits 10 to 7 of the identifier are the node ID, bits 6 to 1 the command ID, bit 0 the error bit.
  • Node ID, bits 10 to 7: which driver, 0 to 15. A driver acts only on frames with its own node ID and sends with it. Set it with #CANID or Send_CAN_ID and save; every driver ships as node 0. Use 0 to 13: the bootloader reserves 14 and 15, and a driver on one of those cannot be updated over CAN.
  • Command ID, bits 6 to 1: which message, 0 to 63. The CAN reference lists all of them.
  • Error bit, bit 0: in a frame from the driver, 1 while any error is active. In a frame from the host it is ignored.

So a host sends Send_data_pack_1 (command 2) to node 3 with the identifier (3 << 7) | (2 << 1) = 0x184, and the driver answers with command 3 under (3 << 7) | (3 << 1) | error. A lower node ID wins the bus arbitration.

Multi-byte values are big-endian: the most significant byte is in data[0] and goes first. Floats are IEEE 754 single precision. Flags inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit.

docs.title: Three kinds of message
docs.text:
• Send_…: the host sends data. Some of these are answered (a motion command with Respond_data_pack_1, the gripper command with Respond_Gripper_data_pack); most are not.
  • Send_Respond_…: the host asks for data with a remote frame (the RTR bit set, no data) carrying the command ID; the driver answers with a data frame with the same command ID.
  • Respond_…: frames only the driver sends: the answers above, and the heartbeat.

docs.title: A control loop
docs.text:
Send Send_data_pack_1 at a fixed rate, 100 Hz to 1 kHz, with the setpoint for this cycle; read Respond_data_pack_1 for the position, speed and current of the last cycle. Every valid motion frame, and every request the driver answers, resets the watchdog; the setting frames (gains, limits, Idle, Clear, Send_Parameter) do not.

So with Send_Watchdog set to a few cycle times the motor stops when the host stops; from firmware 109 it can also hold its position, brake, coast or let a joint down slowly (The watchdog).

A watchdog kept with Send_Save_config runs from power-up: a host that does not start its loop within the watchdog time finds the driver in watchdog error, and clears it with Send_Clear_Error.

The heartbeat is the other way round: Send_Heartbeat_Setup makes the driver send a frame on its own every N ms when it has nothing else to send, so the host can see it is alive.

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant D as Driver
    H->>D: Send_Clear_Error
    H->>D: Send_Watchdog: a few cycle times
    H->>D: Send_Heartbeat_Setup: every N ms
    loop every cycle, 100 Hz to 1 kHz
        H->>D: Send_data_pack_1: the setpoint, with the feedforwards
        D-->>H: Respond_data_pack_1: position, speed, current, the error bit
    end
    D-->>H: heartbeat, whenever nothing else was sent for N ms
    Note over D: no motion frame or status request within the watchdog time: watchdog error, the motor stops

docs.title: Parameters, identity and telemetry
docs.text:
From firmware 109 a host can also:

  • set and read any setting by its number with Send_Parameter and Send_Get_Parameter (IDs 36 and 37, the answer on 38), including the gains and limits in force, which it could not read back before (Parameters and buffers);
  • ask a drive what it is with Send_Respond_Identity (ID 39): product, tool, firmware release, pole pairs, whether it is calibrated;
  • poll temperature, supply voltage, errors and current in one frame with Send_Respond_Telemetry (ID 40);
  • record signals inside the control loop and read them with Send_Buffer_Read (ID 41) (Status and diagnostics).

docs.title: From a PC
docs.text: The CANvas adapter shows up as a serial port and speaks slcan; python-can opens it with bustype='slcan'. The Python library wraps the whole protocol, see With Python. Any CAN adapter that python-can supports works the same way.

docs.title: Several drivers
docs.text: Give each driver its own node ID before you put them on one bus (a bus with two node 0s cannot tell them apart): connect one driver at a time over UART, #CANID 3, #Save. Terminate the first and the last node, and wire the daisy chain as in Power and the CAN daisy chain.

docs.title: Status and diagnostics
docs.text: What the driver tells about itself, from firmware 109: what is in force, who it is, its state in one frame, how long its control loop takes, and recordings of its own signals made inside the control loop. The error flags and what to do about each are on Errors and recovery.

docs.title: What is in force
docs.text:
#Info ends with the section In force:, and parameter 79 holds the same as bits (What is in force: parameter 79):

Line Says encoder table: on, error … deg p-p, measured, off or not measured (Encoder table and anti-cogging) anti-cogging: on (harmonics), on (table), identified, off or not identified, and , saved when it is the saved set current-sense zero trim: the two trims in counts, and whether the zero measured with the bridge switching is in use delay compensation: the commutation delay in µs, or off (Commutation delay compensation) speed estimate: moving average, PLL, … Hz or direct PLL, … Hz (The speed estimate) fast reading / fast PWM: the two register paths of the control loop, on or off input filter:, integral deadband: parameters 74 and 75, or off after #Calangle (parameter 56): what follows a #Calangle: anti-cogging, then save or nothing running: only while one runs: calibration, encoder table, anti-cogging identification, or the runs after the calibration

Before that section #Info prints, beside what it printed before:

  • Build: the git commit the firmware was built from, 7 hex digits. A + after it means it was built with uncommitted changes. Parameter 84 holds the same, and parameter 85 the build time in Unix seconds.
  • Board ID: the chip's unique number, folded into 8 hex digits. It never changes. Also parameter 86.
  • Calibration ID: a new number at every successful #Cal, #Calonly or #Calangle, in 8 hex digits. Save keeps it, and #Default sets it back to 0. Also parameter 87.
  • CAN RX overruns and CAN TX dropped: frames the driver lost because its receive buffer was full, and answers it gave up after waiting 1 ms for a free transmit mailbox. Both should stay 0; they count from power-up. From firmware 109 the CAN controller passes only the frames addressed to the driver's own node ID, and the driver sends from all three transmit mailboxes, so a busy bus costs it less.
  • Product: this firmware, STEPFOC.
  • Current sense zero: the zeros in use, in ADC counts from 2048, measured at start-up with the bridge off (one count is about 1.6 mA), and what the second measurement with the bridge switching found. A zero more than 200 counts from 2048 is not trusted: the driver then uses 2048 and says not measured or out of range. The current sensors need the motor supply. If the driver starts without it (USB plugged in before the supply), it waits up to half a second for the supply, then uses 2048 and says no motor supply at start-up: 2048 used; measured once the supply is there. When the supply comes, the driver measures the zero by itself at rest, coasting for about 80 ms even if it is set to brake, and the line shows the new zeros. The Vbus error the late supply latched stays until #Clear.
  • Tool ID, Watchdog: … ms, action …, fallback …, Settings block 2: ok and Anti-cogging: …, scale … % with whether it is saved.

docs.title: Who the drive is: the identity frame
docs.text:
Send_Respond_Identity (ID 39, a remote frame) answers with the product (1 STEPFOC, 2 Spectral Micro), the tool id, the firmware release, the hardware version, the pole pairs, whether it is calibrated, and eight flags: set up as a gripper, brakes in idle, coils reversed, settings block 2 available, wrong product, current-sense zero measured, anti-cogging saved, switching zero in use (Send_Respond_Identity).

A host can read it before it commands or flashes a drive, to know it talks to the drive it expects.

The tool id says what the drive is built into:

  • 0: none (a joint or a bare driver);
  • 1: an SSG-48;
  • 11 to 33: an MSG (the tens digit the rail, 1 = 100, 2 = 150, 3 = 200 mm; the units digit the stepper, 1 = 21.5, 2 = 40, 3 = 60 mm);
  • 200 to 254: your own tools.

Set it with #Tool or parameter 1 and save.

docs.title: Everything at once: telemetry
docs.text: Send_Respond_Telemetry (ID 40, a remote frame) answers with the temperature, the supply voltage, both error bytes and the current, all from the same moment: one request instead of four, for a host that watches many drives (Send_Respond_Telemetry).

docs.title: The product lock
docs.text:
STEPFOC and the Spectral Micro use the same bootloader and the same file name for their firmware, and each firmware drives the other board wrongly: the Spectral firmware on a STEPFOC drove a coil at about 1.7 A in every mode on the bench.

From firmware 109 a board remembers which product calibrated it, a stamp in the EEPROM written at the first start-up of a calibrated board and at every save.

A firmware that finds the other product's stamp, or no stamp but a calibration its own product cannot make (STEPFOC calibrates only 50, 75, 100 or 125 pole pairs), reads and writes nothing more, drives no pin and starts no control loop.

It stays reachable: it reports an error, Wrong firmware for this board (product lock) in #Error, the wrong_product bit in the error state and the identity, and a warning in #Info. Flash the right firmware and the board runs as before; nothing was written.

#Product shows the stamp. On a board the rule misjudges, #Product claim stamps it as this product and #Product clear removes the stamp; power-cycle after either. Both are UART commands only.

docs.title: How long the control loop takes
docs.text:
The control loop runs every 160 µs (6250 Hz) and has to finish inside that. #Info prints the last loop's time; parameters 66 to 70 give its five sections, averaged over about 64 loops, in 0.1 µs: the checks, reading the encoder, the currents and the supply, the transforms, the control mode with the PWM, and the rest (the capture).

On the bench drive with everything on (anti-cogging, delay compensation, the direct PLL, the encoder table, fast reading and PWM) the loop took about 129 µs of its 160 while the motor turned, 128 µs while it held, 68 µs in idle. What the features cost while turning:

Feature Parameter µs per loop anti-cogging on 37 about 10 commutation delay compensation 64 about 10 encoder table on 53 0.1 moving average instead of the direct PLL 50 −1 sin and cos from the table 65 +1.3 (slower, so off) fast reading off 71 +14 fast PWM off 72 +4

Without the two fast paths the loop would take about 148 µs while turning, too close to 160 for comfort: leave them on. They read the ADC and the encoder and write the PWM by register instead of through the library calls, with every wait bounded; the current noise stayed the same.

docs.title: A capture
docs.text:
The capture records three signals inside the control loop, sample by sample, 1024 samples per channel: what the loop saw and did, which a host polling over the bus cannot see.

Parameters 24 to 33 set it up and report on it, Send_Buffer_Read with kind 0 reads it (Reading the capture; the signals are listed under Capture and histogram). While the encoder table or the anti-cogging run turns the motor, a capture is not armed: the runs use its memory.

A step response, 1024 samples of speed, current and position error, one every 2 loops (0.33 s):

import time
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral

comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)

def read_all(seconds):
    end = time.time() + seconds
    while time.time() < end:
        message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.01)
        if message is not None:
            motor.UnpackData(message, ids)

for number, value in ((24, 4), (25, 1), (26, 7), (27, 2), (28, 1)):
    motor.Send_Parameter(number, value)     # A speed, B Iq, C position error; every 2nd loop; start now
motor.Send_data_pack_1(1000, 0, 0)          # the step: to position 1000
read_all(0.5)
motor.Send_Get_Parameter(32)                # how many samples
read_all(0.1)
count = motor.parameters.get(32, 0)
motor.Send_Buffer_Read(0, 0, count)         # kind 0, from sample 0
read_all(3.0)
for i in sorted(motor.capture):
    speed, iq, position_error = motor.capture[i]
    print(i, speed, iq, position_error)

Trigger 2 records up to an error instead: armed with a pre-trigger, it keeps the moments before a trip, the watchdog's included, and the time after it. The capture calls (Send_Parameter, Send_Get_Parameter, Send_Buffer_Read) need the Spectral-BLDC library 1.21 or newer.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
The drive's microcontroller has 128 KB of flash, of which the bootloader takes 12 KB, and 20 KB of RAM. Firmware 109 uses about 91 % of the 116 KB application flash and 65 % of the RAM for fixed data, which leaves about 7 KB for the stack and the heap.

Parameter 83 (#Par 83, or Send_Get_Parameter(83)) is the margin check: the bytes of that RAM the stack has never reached since start-up. The stack needs about 1.5 to 2 KB; read parameter 83 after the drive has run its hardest work (a calibration, the encoder table, the anti-cogging, sound) and see that plenty is left.

docs.title: A histogram
docs.text:
The histogram adds one signal into 256 bins over the electrical angle or over one motor turn, every control loop, until it is stopped or a bin holds 65535 samples (about 45 minutes): the mean per bin shows what repeats with the angle, such as the cogging current at a steady speed.

Parameter 35 picks the signal, 34 starts it (1 electrical angle, 2 motor turn) and stops it (0), 36 counts the samples, and Send_Buffer_Read with kind 1 reads the count and the sum of each bin. The anti-cogging identification uses it the same way; while it runs, parameters 34 and 35 refuse a write.

docs.title: Errors and recovery
docs.text: When the driver detects a fault it stops the motor, goes to idle, turns the status LED on steadily and sets the error bit in every CAN frame it sends. It stays there until the error is cleared.

docs.title: Seeing the error
docs.text:
• The LED: on and not flashing means error mode (or not calibrated). Three short flashes and a pause is normal operation; fast flashing is calibration.
  • #Error prints In error state! or No errors!, followed by one line per active error.
  • Send_Respond_State_of_Errors returns every flag as a bit; the error bit of any frame says whether there is one.
Normal operation Calibration Error mode

In error mode the LED does not flash: it stays on, as in the photo on the right.

docs.title: The errors
docs.text: Error #Error line Cause What to do Vbus Vbus error the supply voltage is below 9 V or above 29 V (#Vmax, 29000 mV after #Default). From firmware 109 a low voltage is not checked for the first 500 ms after power-up, while the supply ramps up check the supply and the cable; a decelerating motor can push the voltage up Encoder Encoder error the encoder reports no magnet: missing, too far away or too weak magnet distance and type, see The encoder magnet Driver Driver error (undervoltage, thermal shutdown, or overcurrent) reserved: this firmware never raises it, because it does not monitor the driver stage — Velocity Velocity error the speed passed 30,000,000 ticks/s, a fixed threshold that #Vlimit does not change; in practice only a runaway reaches it check the magnet and the calibration Temperature Temp error the thermistor reads more than #Tlim (75 °C by default) or less than −20 °C, with #Term 1. A thermistor that is not plugged in reads far below −20 °C let the motor cool; lower the current limit E-stop Received ESTOP command Send_ESTOP was received clear it when it is safe Watchdog Watchdog error no motion frame or answered request within the watchdog time (Send_Watchdog); what the motor does then is the watchdog's action, see The watchdog the host stopped sending; fix the host, then clear Wrong product Wrong firmware for this board (product lock) from firmware 109: this board was calibrated by the other product (a Spectral Micro firmware on a STEPFOC, or the other way round), so the firmware drives nothing (The product lock) flash the right firmware; it does not clear otherwise Not calibrated Not calibrated the motor has not been calibrated since #Default, or the EEPROM is invalid run #Cal and #Save Current Current error reserved; this firmware never raises it —

docs.title: Clearing
docs.text:
#Clear or Send_Clear_Error clears the flags and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back: a Vbus error at 2 V stays until the supply is right; once the supply is 24 V, one #Clear returns the driver to normal operation.

The calibration error clears only by calibrating (or, for a motor you know is calibrated, #Calibrated 1). A gripper E-stop comes back on every control cycle until its E-stop bit is 0 again: #Gripstop 0, or a Send_gripper_data_pack with the bit clear; then clear. While it is active, #Error prints only In error state!.

docs.title: When the driver does not answer
docs.text:
• No LED at all: no power. Check DC+ and DC− and the cable orientation.
  • LED on, no answer on UART: the baud rate (256000), TX and RX crossed, the adapter's port.
  • No answer on CAN: the node ID, the termination (about 60 Ω across the bus, unpowered), 1 Mbit/s on the adapter.
  • #Info shows -1 or nonsense: with firmware 106 and newer this should not happen, because the driver replaces a damaged configuration block with the defaults at power-up. If it does, #Default, then calibrate again.

Troubleshooting goes through the symptoms one by one.

docs.title: Gripper mode
docs.text: A driver can run a gripper instead of a joint: the same board, with a state machine that moves a jaw to a position between open and closed, at a speed, with a current limit that becomes the grip force, and that reports when it holds something. The MSG gripper is built on STEPFOC this way.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
#Gripper 1
#Save

#Default clears the flag again. A driver in gripper mode still answers every other command; the gripper commands only work with the flag set.

docs.title: Calibrating the gripper
docs.text:
After every power-up the gripper has to find its end stops: #Gripcal or Send_gripper_calibrate. The jaws open until they stop, then close until they stop, slowly and at 500 mA; the positions become 0 (open) and 255 (closed). The driver prints nothing when it is done.

If it has not found both end stops within about 24 s it gives up, and the gripper stays uncalibrated. Check the result with #Gripinfo (Gripper calibrated is: 1) or the gripper_calibrated bit of Respond_Gripper_data_pack: a move is carried out only once the gripper is calibrated. The motor itself must be calibrated (#Cal) and saved before that, once.

While the gripper calibrates, send only empty status polls. A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error or #Clear stops the calibration without a message, and the next one then starts part way through, where the stopped one left off: switch the driver off and on before you calibrate again (known issue KI-7).

docs.title: Moving
docs.text:
Over UART:

#Gripvel 100       speed, 0 to 255
#Gripcur 400       current limit of the move in mA, the grip force
#Grippos 200       go to position 200 (0 open, 255 closed); also activates the gripper

Over CAN, Send_gripper_data_pack carries position, speed and current in one frame with the activate and action bits; the driver answers with Respond_Gripper_data_pack: the position, the measured current, whether it is moving, and the object detection:

Object detection Meaning 0 moving 1 an object was detected while closing: the jaws stopped on it and hold it with the current limit 2 an object was detected while opening 3 the position was reached

An empty Send_gripper_data_pack (0 bytes) only asks for the state. The answer to a 5-byte command goes out before the driver acts on it, so its object detection and error bits are still those of the moment before (KI-6); the answers to the next frames show the new move.

The action bit in the answer is a copy of the last command's action bit and stays 1 after the move ends (KI-8): the object detection tells when it has ended.

Send_gripper_data_pack's E-stop bit raises the gripper E-stop error; #Gripstop 1 does the same over UART. The error stays: while the E-stop bit is 1 the driver raises it again on every control cycle, and #Error prints only In error state!. To recover, clear the bit (#Gripstop 0, or a Send_gripper_data_pack with the bit 0), then #Clear or Send_Clear_Error.

Current

From firmware 109 a gripper move uses the magnitude of the current you give it, at most the driver's 2800 mA; 108 and older used it as sent. The safe range depends on the gripper's mechanics and motor; the gripper's manual gives it.

docs.title: Where the details are
docs.text: The bytes of the two gripper frames are in the CAN reference, the UART commands in the UART reference.

docs.title: Control modes
docs.text:
The driver is always in one control mode. A command that carries a setpoint switches to the mode that uses it; #Idle or Send_Idle switches back to idle. The driver refuses every mode except idle, open loop included, while it is not calibrated or while an error is active.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NotCalibrated: power-up, no saved calibration
    [*] --> Idle: power-up, saved calibration
    NotCalibrated --> Calibration: #Cal
    Calibration --> Idle: success, #Save
    Calibration --> NotCalibrated: a test fails
    Idle --> ControlMode: a setpoint
    ControlMode --> Idle: #Idle, Send_Idle
    ControlMode --> Error: a fault
    Idle --> Error: a fault
    Error --> Idle: #Clear, cause gone

A setpoint is #P, #V, #Iq, #PD or a CAN motion frame, and a new setpoint switches the mode without passing through idle; a fault is any of the errors on Errors and recovery.

ControlMode What the motor does Entered by Setpoint unit Idle nothing: brakes (phases shorted), the default, or coasts (phases open), as set by #Brake / #Coast or Send_Settings; see Braking in idle #Idle, Send_Idle, #Clear, errors — Position holds and moves to a position with the cascade of position, velocity and current loops #P, Send_data_pack_1 (8 bytes) encoder ticks Velocity turns at a speed with the velocity and current loops #V, Send_data_pack_1 (5 bytes) encoder ticks/s Current (torque) applies a current, so a torque, with the current loop alone #Iq, Send_data_pack_1 (2 bytes) mA PD (impedance) behaves like a spring and a damper around a position, with KP and KD #PD, Send_data_pack_PD encoder ticks Voltage torque applies a voltage on the q axis directly, without the current loop: clamped to #Vlim, not current-limited #Uq mV Open loop steps the motor like a plain stepper driver, without the encoder and without a current limit; see Open-loop stepping #Openloop (continuous), #gosteps (a number of microsteps) electrical rad/s; microsteps HALL spins until a sensor on ADDITIONAL2 triggers, then holds the position reached; with a level trigger only while the pin stays at that level #HALL, Send_data_pack_HALL encoder ticks/s Gripper runs the gripper state machine: move to a jaw position with a speed and a current limit #Grippos, Send_gripper_data_pack (with #Gripper 1) 0 to 255 Calibration the calibration routine, and the angle-offset step alone #Cal, #Calangle, #Gripcal —

docs.title: Braking in idle
docs.text:
In idle the driver brakes: it keeps both coils shorted through the driver stage, so the motor resists being turned. It does so at every power-up, and also with an error, which puts the driver in idle.

#Coast (or Send_Settings over CAN) lets the motor coast instead, with the coils open, until the next power-up: #Save does not keep it. #Brake brakes again.

The braking current is not limited

A motor that is turned while it brakes drives its own back-EMF current through the shorted coils, and the current loop does not limit that current. Do not let a load drive a braking motor fast; send #Coast first when the shaft must turn freely.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
• Position is in encoder ticks: 16384 per revolution of the motor shaft, counting up without limit over several revolutions. Positive is counter-clockwise seen from the magnet (the back of the motor).
  • Speed is in encoder ticks per second: 16384 is one revolution per second, 60 rpm.
  • Current is in mA. Torque is current times the motor's Kt, which calibration finds.
  • Feedforward: the 8-byte motion frame carries a speed and a current feedforward beside the position, the 5-byte one a current feedforward beside the speed. They are added after the loops, so a host that knows the trajectory can command it directly and leave the loops to correct the rest. Send 0 when you do not use them.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Ticks (a position, or a speed per second) Pole pairs 50 (1.8° stepper) 75 (1.2°) 100 (0.9°) 125 (0.72°)

As a position: 1.000 turns, 360.0° · as a speed: 60 rpm · the practical maximum for 50 pole pairs is about 720 rpm

Kt in Nm/A (what #Kt prints) Current in mA

Torque: 0.21 Nm, 21 N·cm

The units of this page, with your numbers: 16384 encoder ticks per turn, the practical speed limit from the electrical frequency the control loop can follow (Ratings and limits), and the torque as Kt times the current.

docs.title: Open-loop stepping
docs.text:
#Openloop and #gosteps drive the coils like a plain stepper driver, without the encoder in the loop. Like every other mode, they need a calibrated driver without errors.

  • #Openloop 50 turns the field at 50 electrical rad/s and keeps turning until another command. On a motor with 50 pole pairs that is 50 ÷ (2π × 50), about 0.16 revolutions per second.
  • #gosteps 64 makes 64 microsteps, then goes to idle; a negative number goes the other way. #microstep (16 by default) is the number of microsteps per electrical cycle, which is four full steps: with 16, #gosteps 16 turns a 1.8° motor by 7.2°. #stepinterval (1000 µs by default) is the time between two microsteps, rounded down to whole control cycles of 160 µs.
  • #Openv (5000 mV by default) is the voltage both put on the coils.

None of these settings is saved.

Open loop is not current-limited

Open loop applies a voltage, not a current, and #Ilim does not apply. At standstill and low speed the coil current is about #Openv ÷ R: the default 5000 mV drives about 4.5 A through a 1.1 Ω coil, more than the driver's 2.8 A and the motor's rating. Set #Openv to the rated current × R first (2 A × 1.1 Ω = 2200 mV), and keep the test short.

docs.title: Positive rotation
docs.text: Figure 6.1: Positive rotation is counter-clockwise looking at the encoder magnet. A positive current turns the motor that way, a positive speed too, and the position grows.

docs.title: Which mode am I in?
docs.text:
#Mode prints the mode: Idle mode, Position control, Speed control, Current control, PD control, Open loop, Gripper mode or Gripper calib mode.

In this firmware release the voltage-torque mode reads Gripper mode too (a leftover label), and HALL mode, the angle-offset search (#Calangle), open-loop steps (#gosteps), gripper mode and the encoder-table run print nothing. The behaviour of the motor is the reliable check there.

docs.title: Working in Motor GUI
docs.text: Everyday use of the driver from Motor GUI: moving the motor, watching it, recording what it does, running several motors, and the few things that only work from the console.

docs.title: Moving the motor
docs.text:
The jog controls send setpoints in the matching control mode: Jog velocity turns the motor at a speed in encoder ticks per second (16384 is one revolution per second), Jog position moves it to a position in ticks, Jog current applies a torque in mA.

Send setpoint sends a value in the mode the driver is in. Idle stops the motor; Control modes says what each mode does. With Live stream while dragging the setpoint follows the slider, which is the quickest way to feel a tuning change.

docs.title: Watching it
docs.text: The plots show position, speed and current as the driver reports them. Pan and zoom to a move; hover for the value. A step in the position setpoint shows overshoot and settling at once, a speed step shows the velocity loop's response; Current limit and loop tuning uses them step by step.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text: A recording keeps the telemetry stream to a file: New recording, run the move, Stop recording. Record the response before and after a tuning change to compare them, or a failure to attach to a bug report (Report a problem).

docs.title: Clearing errors
docs.text: The errors the driver reports are listed with the state; Clear errors sends what #Clear does. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back; Errors and recovery says what each one needs.

docs.title: Several motors
docs.text:
Over the CANvas adapter the GUI sees every driver on the bus and addresses each by its node ID.

Give each driver its own ID over the serial adapter first (the CAN node ID in the settings, then Save), terminate the first and the last node, and set a watchdog (Watchdog ms) on a bus that drives something that must not run away: Power and the CAN daisy chain, Over CAN.

docs.title: Gripper
docs.text: A driver in gripper mode shows the gripper controls: calibrate the jaws, a position from open to closed, a speed, a current limit, and the state the gripper reports. No gripper connection means the driver is not in gripper mode or not on the bus. Gripper mode.

docs.title: Firmware updates
docs.text: Firmware update lists the releases from GitHub and flashes one through the bootloader; on a bus, Scan bootloaders finds the boards. Updating through the bootloader.

docs.title: The console
docs.text: Anything the GUI has no control for is one # command away in the console, with the driver's answer below it; the whole set is in the UART commands reference. The cyclic output (#Cyc) is what the GUI's telemetry stream uses over serial, so do not start it by hand while the plots run.

docs.title: Reading a fault
docs.text:
1 2 3 4

Figure 6.3: 1. Errors state: a fault is active. 2. Errors tab: inspect individual flags. 3. E-stop error: 1 identifies the latched fault in this simulation. 4. Clear errors: clear it after removing its cause; a persistent cause returns on the next update. Screenshot captured from Mock CAN (demo).

Check

After recovery the fault flag returns to 0 and the state shows No errors. If it returns, stop and follow Errors and recovery.

docs.title: With Python
docs.text: The Spectral-BLDC library wraps the CAN protocol: one method per message, and the driver's answers unpacked into attributes. It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS with any adapter python-can supports, such as the CANvas adapter over slcan.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
In a virtual environment:

WindowsLinuxmacOS 

py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install Spectral-BLDC
The CANvas adapter is COM and a number (Device Manager, Ports (COM & LPT)): channel='COM41'.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install Spectral-BLDC
sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER     # access to the serial port; log out and in again once
The CANvas adapter is /dev/ttyACM0 (ls /dev/ttyACM* lists it): channel='/dev/ttyACM0'.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install Spectral-BLDC
The CANvas adapter is /dev/cu.usbmodem and a number (ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* lists it): channel='/dev/cu.usbmodem1101', with your number.

Check

python -c "import Spectral_BLDC" returns without an error message.

The source and the examples are in Spectral-BLDC-Python. For joints with a gear ratio and an offset, the Source Robotics Toolbox (pip install SourceRoboticsToolbox) turns encoder ticks into joint angles.

docs.title: The first program
docs.text:
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# the adapter: a CANvas on COM41 (Windows) or /dev/ttyACM0 (Linux), 1 Mbit/s
comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
# the driver with node ID 0
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)

motor.Send_Clear_Error()

# A configured, calibrated motor with a clear shaft: command one turn for five seconds.
# Each command requests a fresh position/speed/current reply; heartbeat is not required.
try:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 5.0
    next_cycle = time.monotonic()
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        motor.Send_data_pack_1(Position=16384, Speed=0, Current=0)
        reply_deadline = min(deadline, time.monotonic() + 0.02)
        while time.monotonic() < reply_deadline:
            message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(
                timeout=max(0.0, reply_deadline - time.monotonic()))
            if message is None:
                print("No motion feedback in this cycle; check the bus and node ID")
                break
            if ids.node_id != 0 or ids.command_id != 3:  # Respond_data_pack_1
                continue
            motor.UnpackData(message, ids)
            print(motor.position, motor.speed, motor.current, ids.error_bit)
            if ids.error_bit:
                raise RuntimeError("Driver fault: inspect State_of_Errors before retrying")
            break
        next_cycle += 0.02
        time.sleep(max(0.0, next_cycle - time.monotonic()))
finally:
    motor.Send_Idle()                    # also on Ctrl-C; the shaft no longer holds torque

receive_can_messages returns the raw python-can message and a tuple with the node ID, the command ID and the error bit of the identifier; UnpackData decodes the message into the attributes the message carries.

This example resends the same setpoint at 50 Hz for five seconds, prints only matching motion feedback, and puts the motor in idle when it ends. Idle releases torque: support any attached mechanism before running it. A missing reply is reported without claiming that a move finished. Configure and calibrate the driver first (Quick start).

Check

The program prints a line of position, speed, current and error bit for each cycle, the position moves to 16384 and the error bit stays 0. No motion feedback in this cycle means no answer came back: the port, the node ID and the bus, see Over CAN.

docs.title: What is where
docs.text:
Library call Message What you get back Send_data_pack_1(Position, Speed, Current) Send_data_pack_1 position, speed, current Send_data_pack_PD(...) Send_data_pack_PD position, speed, current Send_Respond_Encoder_data() Send_Respond_Encoder_data position, speed (32-bit) Send_Respond_State_of_Errors() Send_Respond_State_of_Errors the error attributes Send_gripper_data_pack(...) Send_gripper_data_pack gripper_position, gripper_current, the gripper state bits Send_Limits(...), Send_Velocity_Gains(...), ... the setting messages nothing; Send_Save_config() keeps them

The complete map of calls to messages is in the Python library reference, and each message's bytes in the CAN reference.

docs.title: Several motors
docs.text:
One CanCommunication per bus, one SpectralCAN per driver with its node ID. Send to each, then read the bus: every answer carries the node ID in ids.node_id, so route it to the right object.

motors = [Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=i, communication=comms) for i in range(3)]
for m in motors:
    m.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
for _ in motors:
    message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.1)
    if message is not None:
        motors[ids.node_id].UnpackData(message, ids)

The Guides build on this: a quadruped leg, gravity compensation, bilateral teleoperation.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text: From firmware 109 the driver plays sound through its motor: tones, chords, tunes from a queue it plays by itself, and recorded sound such as speech. A current at an audio frequency in the windings makes a small force at that frequency, and the motor, and above all whatever it is fixed to, radiate it as sound.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Where: the driver adds the sound to its output voltage, after the current loop. By default it goes on the q axis (parameter 82 = 1), where it makes torque: the rotor rocks at the tone's pitch. On the bench that was much louder than the d axis (82 = 0), which makes no torque at all.
  • When: only while the driver holds or moves: position, velocity, current or PD mode. Idle, or any error, stops all sound. A joint keeps holding its pose while it plays.
  • Tones: up to 4 at once (channels 0 to 3), a chord on one motor, each with its own pitch, loudness and length.
  • Loudness is given as a current, in mA. The coil's impedance rises with the pitch (√(R² + (2πfL)²), from the motor's R and L), so the same voltage would sound much quieter high than low; the driver turns the current into the voltage that pitch needs, and a note is as loud low as high.
  • Pitch: 20 Hz up to just below 3125 Hz, half the 6250 Hz control loop. Tones are clean up to about a third of the loop rate; melodies sit well between C4 and C6 (262 to 1047 Hz).
  • The queue: 31 events, each setting one channel's pitch and loudness and then waiting. The control loop plays them with loop-exact timing, so the host's own timing never reaches the music: it loads the queue and starts it.
  • Samples: recorded sound, 8 bits, played from a 1024-place buffer at a rate the host sets, up to the loop rate. Speech comes through recognisable but muffled: the telephone band reaches 3400 Hz, the motor about 3 kHz.
  • The cap: all sound together is limited to the voltage of parameter 81, 2000 mV by default; 0 refuses sound. None of the sound settings is saved.

docs.title: A tone over UART
docs.text:
#Tone 440,250,1000      440 Hz, 250 mA, 1000 ms
#Tone 880,200,0         until stopped
#Tone off               stops all sound

From idle, a calibrated driver first holds the position it is at and says so (Holding the position while it plays (#Idle releases it)); #Idle releases it afterwards. Left out, the loudness is 200 mA and the length 500 ms.

Tone: not played means the driver is not calibrated or in an error, the pitch is outside 20 Hz to half the loop rate, or parameter 81 is 0.

docs.title: Over CAN and from Python
docs.text:
Send_Sound (ID 44) carries every operation: a tone now, an event for the queue, play the queue, play the samples, stop. Send_Sound_Samples (ID 45) fills the sample buffer (Sound in the CAN reference). The Python calls below need the Spectral-BLDC library 1.21 or newer, as does its music module (note names, ringtone melodies, MIDI files, WAV files).

Over CAN the host makes the driver hold first, for example with a position frame to where the motor is:

import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
from Spectral_BLDC import music

comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)


def read_answers(seconds=0.1):
    message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=seconds)
    while message is not None:
        motor.UnpackData(message, ids)
        message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.005)


motor.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()                # where the motor is
read_answers()
motor.Send_data_pack_1(motor.position, 0, 0)     # hold it there
read_answers()

motor.Send_Tone(440, current_mA=250, duration_ms=1000)        # one tone
for channel, note in enumerate(('C4', 'E4', 'G4')):            # a chord: three channels at once
    motor.Send_Tone(music.note_hz(note), current_mA=200, duration_ms=1500, channel=channel)

A tune goes into the queue and plays by itself. A melody becomes two events per note (the note, then a short silence, so repeated notes are heard as two), so up to 15 notes fit at once:

name, melody = music.parse_rtttl('scale:d=8,o=5,b=120:c,d,e,f,g,a,b,c6')
for channel, freq, current, wait in music.melody_events(melody, current_mA=250):
    motor.Send_Sound_Event(freq, current, wait, channel=channel)
motor.Send_Sound_Play()

For a longer tune, keep loading events while it plays: bits 0 to 7 of parameter 80 say how many are still queued. music.read_midi reads a MIDI file, music.split_voices splits it into lines for the four channels, and music.lines_events makes the queue's events from them.

Recorded sound: convert a WAV file to samples at the rate the motor plays, fill the buffer, start it, and keep it filled:

rate = 3125
samples = music.wav_samples('hello.wav', rate, coil_tau_s=0.0026 / 1.1, clip_percentile=0.95)
motor.Send_Samples(samples[:1000])               # fill the buffer first
motor.Send_Samples_Play(rate, full_scale_mV=2000)
sent = 1000
while sent < len(samples):
    motor.Send_Get_Parameter(80)
    read_answers(0.02)
    buffered = (motor.parameters.get(80, 0) >> 8) & 0x7FF
    room = 1000 - buffered
    if room > 0:
        motor.Send_Samples(samples[sent:sent + room])
        sent += room

coil_tau_s is the coil's L ÷ R (here 2.6 mH and 1.1 Ω): the function raises the high frequencies the coil would otherwise swallow, and clip_percentile levels speech so that it plays about four times louder.

At 3125 samples a second a driver takes about 391 frames a second, some 5 % of the bus. When the buffer runs dry the playing stops and bit 27 of parameter 80 says so.

Send_Sound and Send_Sound_Samples do not reset the watchdog: with a watchdog set, keep sending a status request while the sound plays.

docs.title: Limits and care
docs.text:
• Fix the motor to something that rings. A box or a table is far louder than a motor in free air, and a loose motor jumps and distorts the sound. On the bench a bare NEMA 17 was taped down.
  • Keep tones short and moderate. #Tone and Send_Tone default to 200 mA; the bench played notes at 250 mA. The sound current comes on top of the holding current and heats the motor like any other current; a motor is made to turn, and long loud tones are hard on it.
  • On the q axis a tone is a small torque ripple: a held joint vibrates slightly at the tone's pitch. Choose the d axis (parameter 82 = 0) when that matters; it is quieter.
  • The cap, parameter 81, limits all sound together; the output also clamps at the supply voltage.

On the bench (2026-11-08, STEPFOC, a bare NEMA 17 taped down), tones, scales, a tune from the queue, four-note chords and streamed speech all played. The q axis was much louder than the d axis, speech was audible but muffled, and there were no errors, no warming and only small vibrations.

docs.title: The arm as an instrument
docs.text:
Every joint of a robot can play its own line, and because the sound rides on top of the control, the arm keeps holding its pose while it plays.

Load each driver's queue first, then start them one after another: the starts are meant to fall within about a millisecond of each other, and from then on each driver keeps its own time (whether they stay together over a whole song is still to be measured).

Split a MIDI file into as many lines as there are channels, four per driver, and give each driver its four. Through a gearbox the sound changes with the joint; try each joint's range. Playing on an assembled arm has not been tested yet.

docs.title: Checking what plays
docs.text: Parameter Says 79, bit 24 sound is playing 80 bits 0-7 events queued, 8-18 samples buffered, 24 a tone sounds, 25 the queue plays, 26 samples play, 27 the samples ran dry 81 the sound's voltage cap, mV 82 the axis: 1 q, 0 d

docs.title: Over UART
docs.text: The serial port is the interactive way to use the driver: you type a command, the driver answers in text. It is the only way to calibrate, and the quickest way to try a setting. For real-time control of several motors use CAN.

docs.title: The protocol
docs.text:
A command is #, a name, optionally a space and one argument (a number, a word, or numbers separated by commas), and a line ending:

#P 16384
#P
#Cal
  • The name is case-sensitive and matches the firmware's spelling exactly (#Kpiq, not #kpiq); at most 19 characters, the argument at most 19 characters and without spaces (#WdFb 2000,0,1000,2). Firmware 108 and older allowed 20 characters for both together.
  • The line ends with LF (\n); a CR before it is accepted. Terminals send CR+LF when you press Enter, with the setting described in The serial terminal.
  • A Set/Get command with a number sets the value and prints it; without a number it only prints it. #P 16384 moves to position 16384 and prints the position; #P prints the position.
  • An action command takes no number: #Cal, #Save, #Idle.
  • A name the driver does not know is answered with Unknown command (firmware 106 and newer). In firmware 108 and older a few names the parser accepted had no handler and got no answer; from 109 a name is either a command or answered Unknown command.
  • 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V.

docs.title: The driver only answers
docs.text: The driver never sends anything on its own, except with the cyclic commands: #Cyc 100 makes it print position, speed and Iq every 100 ms as $ <position> <speed> <Iq> (for BetterSerialPlotter), #Cyca 100 as Position:x,Speed:y,Iq:z (for the Arduino plotter); #Cyc or #Cyca without a number stops it.

docs.title: Typical sessions
docs.text:
A first test after calibration:

#Ilim 1500        current limit for the motor
#V 16384          one revolution per second
#V 0
#P 0              back to the start
#Idle

Tuning:

#Kpv 0.02
#Kiv 0.001
#V 30000
#Save

Status:

#Info
#Error
#Temp
#Vbus

Every command is in the UART reference, grouped by what it does.

docs.title: The watchdog
docs.text:
The watchdog stops the motor when the host stops talking: a host program that crashes, a cable that comes out, a USB adapter that hangs. It is a timer in the driver.

Every valid motion frame and every request the driver answers starts it again; when it runs out, the driver raises the watchdog error and does what its action says. From firmware 109 the action can hold the position, brake, coast, or let a joint down slowly; before, the driver always stopped into its idle behaviour.

docs.title: Setting it
docs.text:
PythonCANMotor GUI 

motor.Send_Watchdog(_rate=100, _action='Hold')   # 100 ms, then hold the position
The library knows all five actions from 1.21: 'Idle', 'Hold', 'Brake', 'Coast' and 'Descend'. 1.20 and older know only 'Idle', 'Hold' and 'Brake'.

Send_Watchdog (ID 15): the time in ms (4 bytes) and the action (1 byte). Or the parameters 6 (time) and 7 (action) with Send_Parameter.

Watchdog ms in the settings.

0 ms switches it off, the default. Set it to a few of your host's cycle times: with a 100 Hz loop, 30 to 100 ms. Send_Save_config keeps it, and a kept watchdog runs from power-up: a host that does not start sending within the time finds the driver in watchdog error and clears it with Send_Clear_Error.

What starts the timer again: Send_data_pack_1, Send_data_pack_PD, Send_data_pack_HALL, Send_gripper_data_pack, the status requests (Send_Respond_…), Send_Get_Parameter and Send_Buffer_Read. From firmware 109 Send_Watchdog (or parameter 6) starts a fresh window, and Send_Save_config starts the timer again too.

What does not: the other setting frames (gains, limits, Idle, Clear, Settings, Send_Parameter) and every UART command (known issue KI-11). While the encoder table or the anti-cogging is measured, the driver feeds it itself.

docs.title: What a trip does
docs.text:
Action Name What the driver does 0 legacy what firmware 108 and older did: idle, which brakes (the coils shorted) unless #Coast or Send_Settings chose coasting 1 hold holds the position the motor had at the trip, for the fallback time; then the after-action 2 brake shorts the coils at once 3 coast leaves the coils open at once: the motor turns freely 4 descend applies the fallback current, but never lets the motor turn faster than the fallback speed, for the fallback time; then the after-action

Any other action byte acts as 0. 0 is also what an unchanged host sends: the Python library's default, and what the PAR6 runtime sends.

Three rules keep a gentler action from softening the response to a real fault:

  • Only a trip of the watchdog alone gets the action. If another error is active as well (E-stop, encoder, supply voltage, temperature, not calibrated, a gripper E-stop), the driver gives the legacy response.
  • Hold and descend take over only from a running motor: position, velocity, current, PD or gripper mode. A driver that was idle when the watchdog ran out stays as idle was.
  • Hold and descend always end after the fallback time, at most 60 s, so a lost host never leaves a motor driven for good. The after-action follows: 0 legacy, 2 brake or 3 coast.

The driver reports the watchdog error the whole time, and Send_Clear_Error (or #Clear) ends the action at once and goes to idle; the next motion frame takes over.

docs.title: Hold
docs.text:
Hold keeps the position loop on the position the shaft had at the trip. Coming from position or velocity mode it keeps the velocity integral too, so a joint under load does not sag at the moment of the trip.

A host that recovers within the fallback time (a USB hiccup) finds the joint where it left it. On the bench a bare NEMA 17 held within ±40 ticks (0.9°) for 5 s while it was pushed by hand, then braked.

docs.title: Descend
docs.text:
Descend applies the fallback current and limits the speed in both directions to the fallback speed. Inside the cap the speed limiter's integral relaxes back to zero (within about 0.25 s), so it holds back only what keeps the speed at the cap and never more:

  • a joint under gravity with 0 mA lowers itself at no more than the cap speed and rests on whatever stops it;
  • a gripper with its gripping current keeps its grip, and its jaws cannot slam shut;
  • a free motor with a current turns at about the cap speed (on the bench, 200 mA and a 1000 ticks/s cap: 587 ticks/s on average; the stepper's detents slow it).

It starts with the velocity integral at zero, so gravity can take the joint down.

docs.title: The fallback
docs.text:
Four values, kept by Send_Save_config in settings block 2:

Parameter #WdFb position What Default 2 1st how long hold or descend runs, ms (0 to 60000) 2000 3 2nd the current descend applies, mA (signed) 0 4 3rd the speed cap of descend, ticks/s (0 to 65535) 1000 5 4th the after-action: 0 legacy, 2 brake, 3 coast 0 TerminalPython 

#WdFb 2000,0,1000,2
#Save
Four numbers, commas, no spaces. #WdFb alone prints them, and #Info prints the watchdog with them.

motor.Send_Watchdog_Fallback(2000, current_mA=0, speed=1000, after='Brake')
motor.Send_Save_config()
Library 1.21 and newer.

docs.title: Choosing an action
docs.text:
• A bare motor on the bench, a conveyor, a wheel: brake (2) stops it fastest; coast (3) lets it run out.
  • A joint that carries a load: hold (1) for a second or two, so a short loss of the host does not move it, then descend (4) with 0 mA for a joint that gravity pulls down, or brake for one it does not. Choose the cap speed for a joint you can still catch by hand.
  • A gripper: descend with the gripping current, its sign the closing direction, keeps an object held.

These suggestions are untested on an assembled robot arm; try the action on your machine before you rely on it. The braking of brake and of the legacy response is not current-limited (known issue KI-15): a load that drives a braking motor fast drives a large current through the coils.

docs.title: Seeing a trip
docs.text: A capture armed with the error trigger (parameter 28 = 2) records the moments before and after a trip, the watchdog's included: Status and diagnostics.

docs.title: Firmware
docs.text: The driver's firmware is open source and released as numbered builds. A driver shipped with firmware 105 or newer carries a bootloader and updates itself over UART or CAN, and so do some drivers shipped before 105, which report 103 (Drivers that report 103 says how to tell). A driver without the bootloader needs it installed once with a programming adapter.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Releases and versions: how releases are numbered, how to see which one a driver runs, what the release notes contain
  • The bootloader: what it is, how the driver boots, how it is entered, its protocol and tools
  • Updating through the bootloader: the normal update, with Motor GUI, the bootloader's command-line tool, or a PAR6 control box
  • Upgrading from older firmware: what a driver keeps when it is updated to this release, what works at once and what has to be run
  • Installing the bootloader on an older board: for a driver that runs firmware 103 or older
  • Building from source: PlatformIO, the memory layout, uploading with a programming adapter

The release notes of every release up to the one this site describes are in the appendix, Firmware release notes.

docs.title: Installing the bootloader on an older board
docs.text:
A driver running release 103 or older from the main branch has no bootloader: its firmware starts at the beginning of the flash. A driver that reports 103 may have the bootloader all the same; check first, as in Drivers that report 103.

To run any release from 105 on, which is linked to start above the bootloader, the bootloader must be installed once, with a programming adapter on the JTAG connector. After that, every update goes over UART or CAN.

Warning

Disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter before connecting the programming adapter. The adapter powers the board at 3.3 V.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The programming adapter (an ST-LINK with the 1.27 mm pogo-pin adapter for the JTAG pads), or any ST-LINK, J-Link or OpenOCD-compatible probe wired to 3.3 V, GND, SWDIO and SWCLK.
  • STM32CubeProgrammer or the older STM32 ST-LINK Utility on the PC, with the ST-LINK drivers.
  • The bootloader binary from the bootloader repository's bin/ folder; its README.md names the current file.
WindowsLinuxmacOS

STM32CubeProgrammer or the ST-LINK Utility, and the ST-LINK USB driver (STSW-LINK009) for the adapter.

STM32CubeProgrammer; the ST-LINK Utility runs on Windows only. The adapter needs no driver, but your user needs access to its USB device: install the udev rules that come with STM32CubeProgrammer, or run it with sudo.

STM32CubeProgrammer; the ST-LINK Utility runs on Windows only. The adapter needs no driver.

Figure 7.1: The JTAG pads, marked 3V3, GND, SWCLK, SWDIO. The adapter is pressed onto them; a little pressure makes the contact.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Connect the adapter to the JTAG pads and the PC.
  2. In the programmer, connect to the target (SWD). The STM32F103CB shows up with 128 KB of flash.
  3. Erase the chip, or at least the application region: the old firmware and the bootloader must not overlap.
  4. Program the bootloader binary at address 0x08000000.
  5. Disconnect the adapter, power the driver. The bootloader finds no valid application and waits in bootloader mode, with the LED blinking.
  6. Flash the firmware release through the bootloader, over UART or CAN, as in Updating through the bootloader.
  7. #Info shows the new release. #Default, enter the motor parameters, calibrate, #Save.

Check

#Info prints the release you flashed, and a driver powered up while bl_flash.py list or Motor GUI's Scan bootloaders is polling answers in its first two seconds: the bootloader is there. If the firmware does not start, see Updating through the bootloader: when it fails.

Memory layout

0x08000000–0x080022FF bootloader, 0x08002C00 its configuration page (board ID, the application's CRC), 0x08003000–0x0801FFFF the application (116 KB). The bootloader keeps a magic value in RAM to hand over to the application in about 10 ms on a normal boot.

docs.title: The programmer's settings
docs.text:
In ST-LINK Utility, Target → Settings with SWD and the default frequency works; Target → Program & Verify with the start address 0x08000000. The pictures of the old flashing procedure apply to the connection and the settings dialog:

Settings Programming

The same adapter uploads a firmware you build yourself, see Building from source.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text: The firmware is a PlatformIO project for the Arduino core on the STM32F103CB, in the STEPFOC firmware folder of the firmware repository on the bootloader-version branch.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
1. Install Visual Studio Code and the PlatformIO extension.
  2. Clone the repository and check out bootloader-version.
  3. Open the STEPFOC firmware folder in VS Code; PlatformIO fetches the platform (ststm32@15.4.1) and builds with the PlatformIO Build button or pio run. The image is .pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin.

The project is linked for the bootloader: VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000, the linker script ldscript_bootloader.ld, the upload offset 0x08003000 and a maximum size of 118784 bytes, in platformio.ini. A build that exceeds the size fails to link.

Check

PlatformIO ends the build with SUCCESS, and .pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin is there. If it fails, the first error above the summary names the cause.

docs.title: Uploading
docs.text:
PlatformIO runs on Windows, Linux and macOS alike. On Linux, an upload with the programming adapter also needs PlatformIO's udev rules (99-platformio-udev.rules, in the PlatformIO documentation), and a serial port the dialout group.

  • Through the bootloader: flash the built firmware.bin with bl_flash.py or Motor GUI as in Updating through the bootloader. This is how a release is installed, and works on any driver with the bootloader.
  • With the programming adapter: Upload in PlatformIO uses ST-LINK and writes the image at 0x08003000. It leaves the bootloader alone, but it does not update the image CRC the bootloader keeps; see the warning below. The serial monitor (the plug icon) opens the UART at 256000 with send_on_enter, so you can type commands to the driver from the same window.

After an ST-LINK upload the firmware does not start

At every power-up the bootloader checks the firmware against the CRC it stored at the last flash through the bootloader. After an upload with the programming adapter that CRC no longer matches, so the bootloader stays in bootloader mode, with the LED blinking, instead of starting the new firmware. Flash the same firmware.bin once more through the bootloader to recover. Once the bootloader is on the board, install every firmware through it.

Figure 7.2: Build, upload and the serial monitor in PlatformIO's status bar.

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text: src/constants.h FIRMWARE_VERSION, the CAN command IDs, the EEPROM map, the loop and PWM frequencies src/common.h the controller and PID structures with their defaults src/communication.cpp the UART command handlers src/communication_CAN.cpp the CAN receive switch and the transmit functions src/SerialPacketParser.cpp the UART parser: it splits a line into the command and its argument (up to 108 it also kept the list of names it accepted) src/motor_control.cpp the control loops, the calibration routine, the gripper state machine src/bootloader_config.cpp the vector table offset and the reset into the bootloader release_guide.md how a release is cut: version bump, build, tag, GitHub release with firmware.json

docs.title: Making a release
docs.text: release_guide.md in the repository is the procedure: bump FIRMWARE_VERSION, build, commit the source change, tag V<number>, create the GitHub release with the image, firmware.json and the release notes. This site's tools/sync_firmware.py reads a release by its tag; the version box names the release.

docs.title: A firmware for a board without a bootloader
docs.text: The main branch builds a firmware linked at 0x08000000 for boards that have no bootloader. It stops at release 103 and is not maintained; install the bootloader instead, Installing the bootloader on an older board.

docs.title: Releases and versions
docs.text: A firmware release is a number: 103, 105, 106, … Every release is a tag V<number> in the firmware repository and a GitHub release that carries the image stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin, a manifest firmware.json with the image's size, SHA-256 and the commit it was built from, and the release notes. The notes are the firmware's changelog; the appendix collects them.

docs.title: Which release does my driver run?
docs.text:
#Info

prints Software version: <number> among the rest; Motor GUI shows the same number in the driver's identity, and over CAN Send_Respond_Device_Info returns it as the third byte. From firmware 109 Send_Respond_Identity returns it too, as a 16-bit number, with the product it was built for.

From firmware 105 the number is the build's own version. Before that it was read from the EEPROM, where the last #Default wrote it, so it names the firmware that last restored the defaults, not necessarily the one running: 101 and 102 write 101, 103 writes 103.

docs.title: Drivers that report 103
docs.text:
A driver that reports 103 runs either release 103 from the main branch, without a bootloader, or an early build of the bootloader-version branch, which also writes 103 and runs above the bootloader. Some drivers were shipped with the bootloader before release 105. Which image those carry was not recorded: most likely 103, built for the bootloader.

To tell whether yours has the bootloader:

  • Watch the LED as you switch the driver on: with the bootloader it blinks for about two seconds before the firmware starts.
  • Or power it up while bl_flash.py list or Motor GUI's Scan bootloaders is polling: a driver with the bootloader answers in its first two seconds.

With the bootloader, update it to the current release as in Updating through the bootloader; the release it ran before does not matter then. Without one, install it first: Installing the bootloader on an older board.

docs.title: Which release does this site describe?
docs.text: The one in the version box on the landing page and in the version selector in the header. When a newer release changes what a page says, a new version of the site is published and the previous one stays reachable from the selector. The compatibility table says which releases go with which bootloader, Python library and PAR6 runtime.

docs.title: The Spectral Micro counterpart
docs.text:
A change that applies to both drivers comes to the Spectral Micro too. From release 109 the two drivers share their version numbers and are released together (the Spectral Micro went from 107 straight to 109; there is no Spectral Micro 108).

Before, the numbers did not always match: STEPFOC 108 went with Spectral Micro 107. The compatibility table lists the pairs.

docs.title: The two branches
