docs.text:
Releases from 105 on are built from the bootloader-version branch of the repository, whose firmware is linked to run above the bootloader. The main branch holds the firmware of release 103 and earlier, linked to run without a bootloader, and is not updated.

A board running 103 is documented by version 103 of this site; to move it to a current release, see Installing the bootloader on an older board.

docs.title: The bootloader
docs.text:
Every driver shipped with firmware 105 or newer carries a small bootloader in the first 12 KB of its flash.

It starts the firmware on a normal boot, and it loads a new firmware over UART or CAN when a host asks, so a driver is updated without a programming adapter and without opening anything. The bootloader is open source: stm32f103c-bootloader, shared with the Spectral Micro.

docs.title: Memory layout
docs.text:
Address Contents 0x08000000 – 0x080022FF the bootloader (about 9 KB) 0x08002C00 – 0x08002FFF the bootloader's configuration page: the board ID, the firmware's page count and CRC, the bootloader's build version 0x08003000 – 0x0801FFFF the firmware (up to 116 KB) RAM 0x20001000 a magic word the bootloader sets to hand over to the firmware

The firmware is linked to start at 0x08003000 and sets its vector table there (VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000); the first 0x3000 bytes belong to the bootloader and the firmware never touches them.

docs.title: What happens at boot
docs.text:
1. On a reset, the bootloader runs first. If the magic word is in RAM and the reset was a software reset, it checks the firmware's stack pointer and reset vector and jumps straight into the firmware: about 10 ms, the normal boot.
  2. Otherwise it initialises the clocks, CAN, UART and its watchdog, and listens for a host for 2 s. The LED flashes three times at the start, then blinks while the bootloader listens, faster while a host talks to it.
  3. With no host, and a firmware whose stored CRC is valid, it sets the magic word and resets; the next boot takes the fast path.
  4. With a host talking, it stays as long as the host keeps talking: 3 s after the last command, 60 s once a flash is in progress. Any PING resets the timer.
  5. With no valid firmware (never flashed, or a flash that was interrupted), it stays in bootloader mode and waits, with the LED blinking; the driver answers nothing on #Info.

docs.title: Entering the bootloader
docs.text:
• From the firmware: #Reset over UART or Send_Reset (command 14) over CAN. Since firmware 105 both reset the driver into the bootloader's 2 s window; the host tools send them for you.
  • At power-on: the 2 s window after every power-up, if the host is already polling.
  • Always, when there is no valid firmware.

docs.title: The board ID
docs.text:
The bootloader has a board ID of its own, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. 14 and 15 do not exist for it: its command frame, identifier 0x700, decodes as node 14 in the firmware's identifier scheme, so those two node IDs are reserved.

Give drivers node IDs 0 to 13. The firmware accepts #CANID 14 and 15, but the bootloader then keeps its old board ID and a firmware update over CAN cannot reach the driver.

The firmware keeps the board ID in step with its CAN node ID when the configuration is saved: #Save or Send_Save_config writes the node ID into the bootloader's board ID, so a driver answers the host tools under its node ID.

A node ID that is set but not saved is not the board ID yet. A replacement board ships as ID 0; two boards with the same ID on one bus corrupt each other's flash stream, so give the new board its ID alone on the bus first (set-id in the host tool).

docs.title: Transports and protocol
docs.text:
Over CAN (1 Mbit/s, standard 11-bit identifiers) the host commands on identifier 0x700 with 8 data bytes (board_id, cmd, two parameters). The board replies on 0x701 + board_id with 5 bytes (board_id, cmd, error code, a 16-bit parameter).

The firmware image streams in bulk frames on (board_id << 7) | sequence, 16 frames of 8 bytes per chunk, with no reply per frame.

Over UART (256000 baud) the same commands travel in framed packets [0xBB][CMD][LEN][BOARD_ID][DATA…][CRC16] with the same 5-byte reply, but the first four have other numbers.

Commands over CAN: WBUF (1), WPAGE (2), WCRC (3), PING (4), SET_ID (5), ERASE_APP (6), STREAM_BEGIN (7), STREAM_STATUS (8).

Over UART: PING (1), WBUF (2), WPAGE (3), WCRC (4), and the others as over CAN, plus STREAM_DATA (9), which carries the stream frames. Error codes: 0 OK, 1 invalid offset, 2 invalid CRC, 3 flash write failed, 4 invalid page number.

A flash is: ping, reset the firmware if it answers, ping until the bootloader answers, ERASE_APP (about 3.5 s), then for each 1 KB page STREAM_BEGIN, 8 chunks of 16 frames, STREAM_STATUS, WPAGE with the page's CRC32; finally WCRC with the page count and the image's CRC32.

The bootloader stores the CRC and reboots into the new firmware. The full wire protocol is in the bootloader repository's docs/PROTOCOL.md.

docs.title: The host side
docs.text:
Tool Transport Use Motor GUI serial adapter (Web Serial) or CANvas one driver on the bench, releases fetched from GitHub host_tools/bl_flash.py in the bootloader repository slcan or gs_usb CAN adapters, or UART scripts, several boards, list, set-id, flash --erase-first the PAR6 control box's flash_motor_firmware.py and the dashboard's Firmware tab the robot's own CAN bus every joint of a robot, from the box

Updating through the bootloader has the commands.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
An interrupted flash leaves an invalid CRC; the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits, so the board is not lost: flash again. A board that answers nothing at all: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch the 2 s window.

The one thing the tools refuse, and that would need a programming adapter to undo, is flashing an image linked for 0x08000000 (a firmware from the main branch) over the firmware region.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text: Boards that run release 103 or older from the main branch have no bootloader; some boards shipped before 105 have it although they report 103 (Drivers that report 103). Installing the bootloader on an older board puts it there once, with a programming adapter at 0x08000000; from then on the board updates like any other.

docs.title: Updating through the bootloader
docs.text:
A driver with the bootloader (firmware 105 or newer) is updated over the UART connector or the CAN bus: the host tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image into it. No programming adapter, and nothing to open.

Before you update

  • Park the mechanism: the motor loses torque during the update and until the new firmware is calibrated and commanded.
  • An update may clear the calibration (the release notes say so when it does); plan to calibrate and #Save afterwards, and note the gains #Info prints. An update to 109 keeps it: Upgrading from older firmware says what changes and what to run.
  • On a bus with several drivers, update each node; a bus with mixed releases behaves unpredictably.

docs.title: With Motor GUI
docs.text: Motor GUI in Chrome or Edge, connected over the serial adapter or the CANvas adapter: choose the release, and the GUI fetches the image and its manifest from the GitHub release, verifies the size and the SHA-256, resets the driver into its bootloader and flashes it. This is the way for one driver on the bench.

docs.title: With the bootloader's command-line tool
docs.text:
The bootloader repository has host_tools/bl_flash.py, which flashes an image over CAN (slcan or candleLight/gs_usb adapters) or over UART:

WindowsLinuxmacOS 
cd host_tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter on COM6, driver with board ID 0
python bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel COM6 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

# over UART on COM7
python bl_flash.py --transport uart --port COM7 --baudrate 256000 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first


cd host_tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0
python3 bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel /dev/ttyACM0 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

# over UART with the serial adapter
python3 bl_flash.py --transport uart --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baudrate 256000 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first
Your user needs the dialout group for both ports (Motor GUI: the port).

cd host_tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0; ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* gives the name
python3 bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel /dev/cu.usbmodem1101 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

# over UART with the serial adapter; ls /dev/cu.usbserial* gives the name
python3 bl_flash.py --transport uart --port /dev/cu.usbserial-0001 --baudrate 256000 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

The tool sends the reset command to the running firmware (#Reset over UART, Send_Reset over CAN), catches the bootloader's two-second window, erases the application pages and streams the image page by page, each page verified by a CRC; list shows the boards in bootloader mode, set-id changes a board's bootloader ID. The image is the stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin from the GitHub release.

Board ID and node ID

The bootloader has its own board ID (0 to 13), kept in its configuration page, separate from the firmware's CAN node ID. The firmware keeps the two in step when the configuration is saved (#Save, Send_Save_config), so a driver's bootloader ID is normally its node ID. After #CANID, save before you flash over CAN.

Check

After the flash, from Motor GUI or the tool, the driver starts the new firmware: #Info prints the release you flashed as Software version, and Motor GUI shows it in the driver's identity. If the driver does not answer, see When it fails.

docs.title: From a PAR6 control box
docs.text: A robot built on the Robot Control Box updates every joint from the box itself, over its own CAN bus, from the dashboard's Firmware tab or with tools/flash_motor_firmware.py; the PAR6 documentation describes it.

docs.title: What happens in the driver
docs.text:
1. The host sends the reset; the firmware reboots into the bootloader.
  2. The bootloader listens for two seconds. With no host it starts the firmware; with a host it stays as long as the host keeps talking (60 s during a flash).
  3. The application pages are erased, then written page by page; each page is checked by a CRC.
  4. The bootloader checks the whole image's CRC, records it, and starts the new firmware.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
A flash that fails or is cancelled part way is not a brick: the stored CRC is invalid, so the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits for a host.

Run the flash again; bl_flash.py list (or a passive scan from the control box) finds the board. A board that answers nothing: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch the two-second window.

An image linked for 0x08000000 (a firmware from the main branch, release 103 and earlier) must never be flashed through the bootloader: it would overwrite the bootloader's own region if the tool did not refuse it. The tools validate the image first.

docs.title: Upgrading from older firmware
docs.text: Firmware 109 changes how the driver measures and controls the motor more than any release before it. This page says what a driver keeps when it is updated to 109, what works at once, what has to be run, and how to go back. Updating through the bootloader is how to flash it.

docs.title: What is kept
docs.text:
Flashing never touches the EEPROM, where the configuration lives (Where it is kept). A driver updated from 106, 107 or 108 starts with everything it had:

  • the calibration: pole pairs, R, L, the angle offset, Kt, KV, the phase order and direction;
  • the CAN ID, the gains, the limits, the watchdog, the heartbeat, the thermistor and the gripper settings.

A driver from 101 to 105, saved before the configuration had checksums, is trusted and sealed at its first start of 109 when it was ever saved; 108 reset a board saved but never calibrated, CAN ID included, and 109 keeps it.

Release 103 and older from the main branch have no bootloader: such a board needs the programming adapter once (Installing the bootloader on an older board).

The new settings start from their defaults: tool id 0, the watchdog fallback 2000 ms / 0 mA / 1000 ticks/s / legacy, parameter 56 = 2.

docs.title: What works at once
docs.text:
These need no measurement and are on from the first start of 109:

  • the direct PLL speed estimate at 60 Hz (The speed estimate);
  • commutation delay compensation, 166 µs (Commutation delay compensation);
  • the fast reading and PWM paths of the control loop;
  • the current-sense zero, measured at every start-up: a STEPFOC that read about 48 mA of current with nothing flowing reads under 1 mA;
  • undervoltage is not checked for the first 500 ms after power-up, so a supply that ramps up slowly no longer leaves a Vbus error behind (overvoltage always is);
  • the watchdog actions: the action byte the host already sends is acted on. Byte 0, what the Python library and the PAR6 runtime send, gives the legacy response, so an unchanged host sees no difference;
  • #Default and a settings reset keep the CAN ID;
  • the new CAN commands and parameters, the identity frame, telemetry, the capture, #Info's In force:, and sound through the motor.

docs.title: What has to be run
docs.text:
These are off after the update, because nothing is saved for them yet; the encoder table and the anti-cogging cannot be switched on before they are measured:

  • the encoder table;
  • the anti-cogging;
  • the current-sense zero trim.

A calibration runs all three (What follows the calibration); so does #Encal all without a calibration.

docs.title: What does not change by itself
docs.text:
• The current gains. The saved Kpiq and Kiiq stay as they are: on a driver calibrated before 109 they are the old gains divided by 7, a loop of about 70 Hz (parameter 49 reads about 71). A calibration computes them again at 160 Hz; so does #Cbw 160 (or parameter 49 = 160), then #Save.
  • The velocity gains. The saved Kpv and Kiv stay as they are, typically 0.007 and 0.0005. Firmware 109 was tuned with 0.02 and 0.001, the PLL speed estimate allowing the higher gain; set them yourself (The velocity loop).

docs.title: The whole upgrade
docs.text:
1. Flash 109 (Updating through the bootloader). #Info prints Software version: 109 and ends with In force:.
  2. Check that the current limit suits the motor (#Ilim), then calibrate, with the shaft free: #Cal. The encoder table (at 80 % of the current limit), the anti-cogging and the trim follow, and everything is saved (about two minutes in all).
  3. Set the velocity gains, for example #Kpv 0.02 and #Kiv 0.001 (a 21.5 mm stepper overshot 95 % at these on the bench; its presets use #Kpv 0.014 and #Kiv 0.00014), then #Save. (Calibration puts the current limit that was in force back when it ends; set #Ilim for your motor before step 2 if it is not.)

Check

#Info prints encoder table: on, anti-cogging: on (harmonics), saved.

With Motor GUI's presets: apply the preset first, then calibrate, then set the velocity gains. On firmware 109 a preset writes the current gains of a 160 Hz loop for its own R and L, the same a calibration computes from them, and its own velocity gains.

On a robot whose joints cannot turn freely, neither the calibration nor the runs after it can be made in place.

There skip step 2: the drive keeps the calibration it has, the new speed estimate, the delay compensation and the current-sense zero work at once, and #Cbw 160 with #Save gives the new current gains. The encoder table and the anti-cogging then stay off.

docs.title: Going back
docs.text:
Flashing 108 or older over 109 is safe for the configuration: the calibration and the first settings block are unchanged, and older firmware ignores everything 109 saved from byte 256 on (tool id, fallback, anti-cogging, encoder table). Flash 109 again and they are all still there.

Not yet tested on the bench

The upgrade from 103 (programming adapter, then the bootloader, then 109) and a downgrade to 108 had not been tested on the bench when this page was written; the rest of what it says was, except where the pages it links say otherwise.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: By symptom. The error flags and what clears them are in Errors and recovery; the faults of the firmware that are known and not yet fixed, with what to do until they are, in Known issues.

docs.title: The motor does not move
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A([The motor does not move]) --> B{Does the driver answer?}
    B -- no --> C[The supply and its polarity, the LED;<br>UART: the baud rate, TX and RX;<br>CAN: the node ID, 1 Mbit/s, the termination]
    B -- yes --> D{Calibrated?}
    D -- no --> E[Enter the motor parameters, then #Cal and #Save]
    D -- yes --> F{An error active? The LED on steadily}
    F -- yes --> G[#Error names it: fix the cause, then #Clear]
    F -- no --> H{A current limit above 0?}
    H -- no --> I[#Ilim to the stepper's rated current, #Save]
    H -- yes --> J[Command a setpoint in a closed-loop mode;<br>#Mode and #Info show the state]

docs.title: The driver does not answer
docs.text: Symptom Check No LED the supply, DC+ and DC−, the power cable's orientation. If the cable was the wrong way round the driver is destroyed LED on, nothing on the terminal 256000 baud; TX to RX and RX to TX; the adapter's port; 3.3 V adapter; the line ending CR+LF LED on, nothing on CAN the node ID; 1 Mbit/s on the adapter; termination (about 60 Ω across CAN H and CAN L with everything unpowered); the CAN cable's orientation Unknown command the name's spelling and case: #Kpiq, not #kpiq; an argument with a space in it (#WdFb 2000,0,1000,2, not #WdFb 2000, 0, 1000, 2) Wrong firmware for this board (product lock), the LED on steadily the other product's firmware was flashed: a Spectral Micro image on a STEPFOC. Flash the STEPFOC firmware; the configuration was not touched (The product lock) the LED keeps blinking and nothing answers after a firmware update the bootloader has no valid firmware, or its CRC does not match after an upload with the programming adapter: flash again through the bootloader, see Updating through the bootloader

docs.title: Motor GUI

docs.title: Low-quality motors
docs.text: Motors with visibly bad windings, an uneven back-EMF or a resistance that differs between the two coils calibrate poorly and run rough. The tested motors are known good.

docs.title: The magnet and the encoder
docs.text:
• The distance is 1 mm. "Magnet Good" from the magnet test does not mean the distance is right, only that the field is strong enough.
  • A magnet touching the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet too far gives a noisy, wrong position.
  • The magnet must be diametrically magnetised and centred on the shaft.

docs.title: The driver gets hot or shuts down
docs.text: The firmware does not monitor the driver stage: if the stage stops on its own, for heat or a short, the motor loses torque and no error is reported. Lower the current limit, give the board airflow, check the motor leads for a short. Near 2.8 A the driver needs cooling.

docs.title: After a firmware update
docs.text:
#Info shows the new release. If the values look wrong or the LED stays on: #Default, enter the motor parameters, #Cal, #Save. A release note says when an update clears the calibration. After an update to 109, Upgrading from older firmware says what to run: a calibration, then the velocity gains.

A Vbus error right after power-up, cleared by #Clear, was the supply ramping up; from firmware 109 a low supply is not checked in the first 500 ms.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text: The faults in the STEPFOC firmware that are known and not yet fixed, and what to do until they are. The pages that describe each part say the same where it matters; this page collects them in one place. Which releases work together is in Versions and compatibility.

docs.title: STEPFOC firmware
docs.text:
Seen in: 109.

What happens What to do More KI-3 The serial number is not read back from the EEPROM at power-up, so #SERNUM, Motor GUI and Send_Respond_Device_Info report 1, and every #Save writes that 1 over the stored number. Tell drivers apart by their CAN node ID. To keep a serial number stored, set it with #SERNUM before every #Save. Saving the configuration KI-4 For anyone reading or changing the source, the start values in common.h are not the factory defaults (the gripper and calibrated flags start at 1, the pole pairs at 50, Max_Vbus at 29500 mV). The EEPROM replaces them at power-up, so a running driver does not show them. Take the defaults from the Defaults page, which lists what #Default writes, or from Set_Default_config() in EEPROM.cpp. Defaults KI-5 While the E-stop bit of the last Send_gripper_data_pack (or #Gripstop 1) is 1, the driver raises the gripper E-stop error again on every control cycle, so Send_Clear_Error or #Clear alone does not clear it. Send a gripper frame with the E-stop bit 0 (or #Gripstop 0) first, then clear the error. Gripper mode: moving KI-6 The answer to a 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack goes out before the driver has acted on the command, so its object detection and error bits are those of the moment before, for example 3 (position reached) from the previous move. Judge the new move by the answers to later frames, or poll with an empty Send_gripper_data_pack. Gripper mode: moving KI-7 A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error or #Clear during the gripper calibration stops it without a message and leaves its counters as they were, so the next calibration starts part way through; it may skip the opening or give up early. Send only empty status polls while the gripper calibrates (up to about 24 s). After an interrupted calibration, switch the driver off and on before you calibrate again. Gripper mode: calibrating KI-8 The action bit in Respond_Gripper_data_pack is a copy of the last command's action bit; the driver never clears it, so it stays 1 after the move has ended. Tell the end of a move by the object detection, 3 position reached, 1 or 2 stopped on an object. Respond_Gripper_data_pack KI-9 Open loop (#Openloop, #gosteps) puts #Openv on the coils without a current limit; #Ilim does not apply. The default 5000 mV drives about 4.5 A through a 1.1 Ω coil. Set #Openv to the motor's rated current times its phase resistance first, and keep open-loop tests short. Open-loop stepping KI-10 The velocity error trips only above a fixed 30,000,000 ticks/s, about 1830 revolutions per second and far above any speed a stepper reaches; #Vlimit does not change it, so it does not catch a motor that runs away. Watch the speed in your host and send Send_Idle or Send_ESTOP when it is wrong. Errors and recovery KI-11 Only motion frames and answered status requests reset the watchdog. Setting frames (gains, limits, Idle, Clear) and UART commands do not, so a host that only configures the driver, or a terminal session with a saved watchdog, ends in a watchdog error. While the watchdog runs, send a status request such as Send_Respond_Encoder_data within every watchdog period. Before you work over UART alone, set the watchdog to 0 over CAN and save. Over CAN: a control loop KI-12 The driver error flag (Driver_error, Driver error in #Error) is never raised. STEPFOC reads no fault output of its driver stage, so a stage that shuts down for heat or a short only makes the motor lose torque, with no error. Watch the current and the position in your host; a commanded motor that goes limp points to the driver stage. Lower the current limit and give the board air. Troubleshooting: the driver gets hot KI-13 #Dir stores a flag that #Info prints as Phase direction, but the control code does not use it: it does not reverse the motor. To make the other direction positive, negate the setpoints and the values you read back in your host. Wiring: phase order and direction KI-14 #Mode prints Gripper mode in voltage-torque mode (#Uq), and nothing at all in gripper mode, HALL mode, the angle-offset search, open-loop steps (#gosteps) and the encoder-table run. In those modes go by the command you sent last, not by #Mode. UART commands: status and utility KI-15 In idle the driver brakes, with the coils shorted, at every power-up and also with an error; #Coast is not kept by #Save. The current a turned motor drives through the shorted coils is not limited. Send #Coast (or Send_Settings) after every power-up if the motor must turn freely in idle, and do not let a load drive a braking motor fast. Braking in idle KI-19 The encoder-table run that follows every #Cal holds a field current of 80 % of the current limit for about 20 s. After #Default the limit is 1700 mA, so the coils then carry about 1.4 A, more than a smaller stepper is rated for. Set #Ilim for the motor before #Cal (a Motor GUI preset sets it). Calibration uses its own limit for its steps and puts yours back before the encoder table runs. Calibration: what follows it

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: What happened Fixed in More KI-1 The current limit of Send_Limits over CAN is used as sent, also above the driver's 2800 mA; only #Ilim over UART clamps it. 109: Send_Limits stops the current limit at 2800 mA and ignores a negative value Send_Limits KI-2 Calibration sets the current limit to 1600 mA and leaves it there, whatever it was before; a #Save right after calibration stores the 1600 mA. 109: calibration puts back the current limit that was in force when it started Calibration: save

docs.title: V109 (2026-11-10)
docs.text: STEPFOC firmware V109 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader. From 109 the STEPFOC and the Spectral Micro share their version numbers. Everything below is described in the manual: STEPFOC docs; what a driver keeps and what to run after the update: Upgrading from older firmware.

docs.title: New features
docs.text:
• Parameters: any setting or read-out by number over CAN (commands 36-38) or #Par: the gains and limits, the watchdog, the current loop, the speed estimate, the tool id and more (parameters 1-87). Identity (39) and telemetry (40) frames.
  • Capture, histogram and buffers (41-43): record three signals from the control loop, read the encoder and anti-cogging tables.
  • Watchdog actions: on a lost host the driver can idle, brake, coast, hold the position, or descend at a capped speed, with a fallback time.
  • Current loop from R, L and one bandwidth (parameter 49, default 160 Hz); the direct PLL speed estimate at 60 Hz by default; commutation delay compensation, 166 µs by default; a position input filter and a velocity-integral deadband.
  • Encoder table and anti-cogging measured on the driver: #Cal runs the calibration, then the encoder table and the anti-cogging identification, and saves; #Calonly is the calibration alone.
  • Sound through the motor: tones, a queue of notes and samples (CAN 44 and 45, #Tone).
  • Identification: #Info and parameters 84-87 report the build (git commit), the board ID and a calibration ID.
  • Settings in blocks with their own checksums; a reset keeps the CAN ID; a product lock refuses a Spectral image on a STEPFOC board.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
• The angle alignment locks the rotor with the calibration current through the coil's resistance (it used a fixed 0.5 V, too weak for small motors with a high coil resistance). On a 20 mm stepper the alignment offset now comes out 6× steadier from run to run; 25 of 25 calibrations passed.
  • Kt and KV are measured in four spins alternating direction at a forced 6 V; a warning only when two same-direction spins differ by more than 5 %.
  • #Cal from a moving motor switches the bridge off first; a failed calibration switches it off at once; an E-stop ends a calibration, and #Cal is refused while one is latched (Cal: not started, the E-stop is latched (#Clear first)); the alignment starts from its first stage after a calibration that was ended from outside. #Calangle is refused while the driver is in error.
  • The current limit is put back when a calibration ends.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Limits: a negative or not-a-number value is ignored by the legacy CAN frames (limits, gains, Kt, voltage limit 0-60000 mV); #Ilim and #Vlimit take the magnitude; the current of a gripper move stays within 0-2800 mA; #PP takes 1-200 pole pairs, only while idle. PWM duties stay between 0 and 100 %.
  • The current-sense zero waits for the motor supply: started on USB before the supply, the driver used a zero about 100 mA off. It now says so in #Info and measures the zero by itself once the supply is there.
  • No undervoltage error while the supply ramps up at power-up.

docs.title: CAN bus
docs.text:
• A gripper poll right after a new move command no longer cancels it as new: object detection reports contact again (it read "at position" while pressing on an object). The same in every release before 109.
  • The current and PD frames set their setpoint and mode together. Length codes above 8 are read as 8; extended (29-bit) frames are ignored.
  • Watchdog: setting its time or a save starts a fresh window; a negative time means off; hold and descend no longer use the last moving loop's delay compensation.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• After #Cal, a host that takes the driver within 3 s drops the encoder-table and anti-cogging runs (they used to start by themselves at the next idle). #Encal and #Cogcal start only on their own words. While such a run turns the motor, a capture is not armed and the histogram is not changed.
  • A storage block whose check fails is read up to three times before its defaults are used. #Info says the anti-cogging is saved only while what is in RAM equals what is stored.
  • The current-loop integrals are cleared whenever the bridge brakes or coasts. The sound queue and sample buffer no longer replay old content after a stop; a pitch the driver cannot play answers Tone: not played.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Python library 1.21 or newer (pip install --upgrade Spectral-BLDC), Motor GUI 0.5.0.
  • The calibration and the settings of 108 are kept. Not tested on the bench for this release: an upgrade from V103 with the ST-Link, and a downgrade.

docs.title: V108 (2026-08-26)
docs.text: STEPFOC firmware V108 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed calibration (#Cal) spuriously failing with Phase order is wrong! on otherwise-healthy motors. The "confirm commutation" pre-check (before the real angle-offset search) commands a pure torque-axis voltage using the not-yet-calibrated encoder angle — depending on a given unit's actual rotor-to-encoder mounting angle, that command could land almost entirely on the wrong axis and produce ~zero torque, failing the check even though nothing was actually broken. Bench-confirmed on a real unit.
  • Fix: retry the pre-check once at a 90° angle bias before declaring failure — guaranteed to land within 45° of the true torque axis on at least one of the two tries. The downstream angle-offset search is unaffected and already independent of this pre-check.
  • Added Spin-confirm delta / Vbus diagnostics to #Cal's failure report, for the rare case both tries still fail.

docs.title: V106 (2026-07-05)
docs.text: STEPFOC firmware V106 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

docs.title: CAN bus
docs.text:
• The controller now drains up to 8 CAN messages per pass instead of just 1, so short bursts (multiple commands sent back-to-back, or a busy multi-node bus) no longer silently drop messages once the 3-deep hardware FIFO fills.
  • A CAN peripheral that fails to initialize no longer bricks the board — UART stays fully usable, only the CAN bus is skipped.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Added a hardware watchdog (100ms). If the control loop ever stops running, the board resets instead of leaving the motor driven at a stale duty cycle.
  • Fixed a bug where Torque_mode could silently overwrite your commanded Iq setpoint when clamping to the current limit — reading it back after clamping now shows what you actually asked for, and raising the current limit afterward immediately restores the original commanded torque instead of requiring the command to be resent.
  • Fixed undefined behavior in a serial-protocol integer conversion (fourBytesToInt).
  • Synced default configuration values that had drifted between two locations in the code, so a fresh #Default and a freshly-flashed board's built-in defaults now agree.

docs.title: EEPROM / configuration integrity
docs.text:
• Added CRC validation over the saved configuration, split into two independent halves: calibration data (resistance, inductance, Kt/KV, angle offset, current-loop gains, etc.) and settings (PID tuning, limits, watchdog config, CAN ID, etc.).
  • This means a corrupted save (e.g. from a power loss mid-write) is detected and safely defaulted instead of silently running with garbage values — and critically, a future firmware update that only adds a new setting can no longer wipe your calibration, since the two are validated independently.
  • Boards upgrading from older, pre-CRC firmware keep their existing calibration automatically — no need to recalibrate after this update.
  • A few unused slots were reserved in the calibration block for upcoming features (e.g. magnet alignment), so those can be added later without another migration.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• PWM output no longer re-resolves which timer/channel it's writing to on every single call (it was doing this 4x per control tick) — resolved once and cached, freeing up ISR headroom.
  • Velocity calculation switched from a floating-point divide to an integer multiply.

docs.title: Usability
docs.text:
• New #Help command — prints a summary of the available commands.
  • Serial now responds with "Unknown command" for unrecognized input instead of silently ignoring it.
  • Calibration now prints progress during the angle-offset search (previously up to ~40 seconds of silence that could look like the board had hung).
  • #Error now also reports driver faults (undervoltage/thermal/overcurrent), not just the other error types.
  • #Info now always reports live ISR execution time, useful for checking control-loop headroom on the bench.

docs.title: Theory corner
docs.text: The control concepts behind the driver's modes, for readers who want to know why a setting does what it does. Nothing here is needed to use the driver; the chapters say what to type.

docs.title: Field-oriented control of a stepper
docs.text:
A hybrid stepper is a two-phase synchronous motor with many pole pairs: 50 for a 1.8° motor, so one mechanical revolution is 50 electrical cycles. A conventional stepper driver drives it blindly: it advances the current pattern one step at a time and relies on the rotor following.

The torque the rotor receives depends on the angle between the stator field and the rotor, the load angle; it is largest a quarter of an electrical cycle ahead of the rotor and zero when the two are aligned.

Because the driver does not know where the rotor is, it keeps full current in the coils at all times, so that even a badly placed field produces enough torque, and it still loses steps when the load angle exceeds 90° electrical.

Field-oriented control (FOC) closes that gap with a measurement of the rotor angle. The encoder on the motor shaft gives the mechanical angle \(\theta\); with the pole pairs \(p\) and the angle offset \(\theta_0\) found by calibration, the electrical angle is \(\theta_e = p\,\theta + \theta_0\).

The two coil currents \(I_A\) and \(I_B\) are transformed into the rotor's frame of reference (the Park transform):

\[ I_d = I_A \cos\theta_e + I_B \sin\theta_e,\qquad I_q = -I_A \sin\theta_e + I_B \cos\theta_e \]

\(I_q\), the quadrature current, is the part of the current that stands at right angles to the rotor field and produces torque: \(\tau = K_t\, I_q\). \(I_d\), the direct current, is aligned with the field and produces none.

Two PI controllers regulate \(I_q\) to the torque demand and \(I_d\) to zero by choosing the voltages \(U_q\) and \(U_d\); the inverse transform turns those into the two coil voltages, applied by PWM at 25 kHz. The loop runs at 6250 Hz.

The consequences are what makes a FOC stepper behave like a servo:

  • the current is only what the torque needs, so the motor runs cool and quiet;
  • the field is always placed where it produces the most torque per ampere;
  • a step is never lost, because the controller knows the rotor position at every instant and works from the error, not from a count of pulses.

Calibration supplies the constants this needs. The pole pairs come from the step angle. The current loop gains follow from the coil's resistance \(R\) and inductance \(L\) and the chosen bandwidth \(\omega_c = 2\pi f_c\) (#Cbw): \(K_p = L\,\omega_c\) and \(K_i = R\,\omega_c\) cancel the coil's electrical time constant and give a first-order response at \(f_c\).

The firmware computes a discrete-time form of these. It keeps \(K_i\) per control loop: Kiiq is about \(R\,\omega_c\) × 160 µs, so do not enter \(R\,\omega_c\) as #Kiiq. Firmware 108 and older divided both gains by 7, a loop of about 70 Hz; 109 uses the formula at 160 Hz.

The angle offset is found by locking the rotor with the stator field and reading where it settles, then refined by a sweep for the offset at which the motor turns alike in both directions. In theory the torque constant follows from the velocity constant: in SI units \(K_t = 1/K_V\) (with \(K_V\) in rpm/V, \(K_t \approx 9.55/K_V\) Nm/A).

The firmware estimates \(K_V\) from the speed the motor reaches at 500 mA per volt of a fixed 6 V limit (the supply voltage, if that is lower) and uses \(K_t = 8.27/K_V\); treat both as estimates.

docs.title: The cascade of loops
docs.text:
Position, velocity and current are controlled by three loops nested inside one another:

\[ \text{position loop: } \omega_d = K_{pp}\,(\theta_d - \theta) \qquad \text{velocity loop: } I_{q,d} = K_{pv}\,(\omega_d - \omega) + K_{iv}\!\int(\omega_d - \omega)\,dt \qquad \text{current loop: } U_q = \text{PI}(I_{q,d} - I_q) \]

The position loop is proportional: its output is a speed demand, limited by the velocity limit. The velocity loop is a PI controller: its output is a current demand, limited by the current limit; the integral term removes the steady-state error a load would otherwise leave. The current loop is the innermost and fastest.

Each loop must be slower than the one inside it, by a factor of five to ten, for the inner loop to look like an ideal actuator to the outer one.

That is why the loops are tuned from the inside out, and why a current loop bandwidth of 160 Hz (the default from firmware 109) leaves room for a velocity loop of a few tens of hertz and a position loop below that.

A command picks where the cascade is entered: a current setpoint uses the current loop alone, a speed setpoint the two inner loops, a position setpoint all three.

The feedforward terms the CAN motion frames carry are added to the demands rather than computed from an error: a speed feedforward is added to the position loop's output, a current feedforward to the velocity loop's output.

A host that knows the trajectory can command it directly and leave the loops to correct what is left, which gives a faster, smoother response than letting the loops produce the whole demand from the error.

An integrator accumulates error over time, and keeps accumulating while the output is at its limit; the overshoot this causes when the limit is released is windup. The velocity loop's integrator is clamped to the current limit, and #Rstint resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which suits a host that sends one setpoint after another in large steps.

docs.title: Impedance control
docs.text:
Impedance control does not prescribe a motion or a force. It prescribes the relation between the two: how much force the motor produces when it is displaced from its setpoint and how fast. The driver's PD mode implements a spring and a damper around the setpoint:

\[ \tau = K_P\,(\theta_d - \theta) + K_D\,(\dot\theta_d - \dot\theta) + K_t\, I_{ff} \]

with the stiffness \(K_P\) in Nm/rad, the damping \(K_D\) in Nm·s/rad, and a current feedforward \(I_{ff}\) for a known load such as gravity. The torque is produced by the current loop (\(I_q = \tau / K_t\)), which is what makes FOC a prerequisite: a stepper driven blindly cannot produce a commanded torque.

The firmware's gains are in its own units. KP is in mA per encoder tick and KD in mA per tick/s (0.14 and 0.0028 by default). KP times the position error in ticks, plus KD times the speed error in ticks/s, plus the feedforward, is the Iq setpoint in mA.

A stiffness \(K\) in Nm/rad is KP = \(K\) × 0.3835 ÷ \(K_t\), with \(K_t\) in Nm/A. A damping in Nm·s/rad converts to KD the same way.

Pushed off its setpoint by an external force \(F\), the motor yields by \(\Delta\theta = \tau_{ext}/K_P\) and pushes back with that force; let go, it returns, with the damper settling the motion. A small \(K_P\) makes a soft joint, a large one a stiff joint; \(K_D\) without \(K_P\) is a pure damper.

The setpoint can move, in which case the virtual spring drags the rotor along a trajectory with a bounded force — the property legged robots, hand-guided arms and anything that touches people or an uncertain environment need.

The impedance loop is also what a position loop is not: the position loop's integral action removes any steady-state deflection and so makes the joint as stiff as the current limit allows, which is the right thing for a machine tool and the wrong thing for a leg.

The full impedance model includes an inertia term, \(M\ddot\theta\); the driver, like most joint controllers, leaves it out, so the apparent inertia is the motor's own.

docs.title: Admittance control
docs.text:
Admittance is the inverse relation: the controller measures the force and commands a motion,

\[ \dot\theta_d = \frac{\tau_{ext} - K\,(\theta - \theta_0)}{B} \]

on top of a stiff position controller. It is the natural form for a machine that has a force sensor and a position loop that cannot be made soft, such as an industrial arm; impedance control is the natural form for a machine whose actuator is a torque source, such as a FOC motor.

The driver has no force sensor and implements impedance; a host that wants admittance behaviour can estimate the external torque from \(K_t I_q\) minus the known load and command positions accordingly, with the limits of that estimate (friction, cogging, the current loop's accuracy).

docs.title: Compliance and stiffness
docs.text:
Stiffness \(K\) is the force per unit of displacement; compliance is its inverse, \(C = 1/K\), the displacement per unit of force. Passive compliance is in the mechanism — a spring, a flexible finger, a belt; active compliance is in the controller — the impedance loop above.

The driver offers three points on that scale: the position mode, stiff up to the current limit; the PD mode, as stiff as \(K_P\); and the current mode, which is no stiffness at all, a torque source the host shapes as it likes.

The current limit #Ilim is a force limit in every mode: the largest torque the motor will produce before it yields, whatever the loops ask. Set it for the motor's rating, and for the mechanism's.

docs.title: Which mode
docs.text: Mode Behaviour under an external force Use Position holds the position up to the current limit, then yields positioning, machines, anything that must not deflect Velocity holds the speed up to the current limit conveyors, wheels, spindles PD (impedance) deflects in proportion to the force, returns when released legs, arms that touch things or people, hand guiding, teleoperation Current (torque) produces the commanded torque, moves as the load dictates a host that closes its own loop, gravity compensation, force-limited pressing

docs.title: What is bilateral teleoperation?
docs.text:
Bilateral teleoperation is a concept that Involves two-way communication where both the operator and the remote device send and receive feedback. The operator controls the device remotely and receives sensory feedback (such as force) from the device to adjust their actions.

The two grippers are virtually coupled to each other, allowing either to act as the master (the haptic interface) or the slave (the manipulator) in the system. We are not using a force sensor at the grippers but are relying on proprioception.

Figure 1: Bilateral teleoperation of two coupled grippers.

Watch these example videos to get a "feel" of the concept:

  • Gripper bilateral
  • 2DOF arm bilateral

What is this used for?

These kind of setup is perfect for: Teleoperation, Imitation learning, Virtual Environments...

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
The magic of this setup is done with these 2 simple formulas.

We got them from amazing Ben Katz paper, creator of mini cheetah quad: Link to the paper

𝜏1,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃2,𝑖 − 𝜃1, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃2,𝑖 − ˙𝜃1,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃1,𝑖)

𝜏2,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃1,𝑖 − 𝜃2, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃1,𝑖 − ˙𝜃2,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃2,𝑖)

Learn more!

You can read more on how it works in our blog post!

docs.text:
This code will run on your PC and it will communicate with the drivers from the CAN adapter.

Advanced example

More advanced code that allows communication over UDP can be found here: Link

import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import SourceRoboticsToolbox as SourceRoboticsToolbox
import time
import numpy as np
from math import pi, sin, cos
from spatialmath import *
from typing import Union, Any, List, Optional, cast

Needed_joint_pos = np.array([100,100]) # If using gripper you will need to adjust this
Joint_reduction_ratio = [1, 1] # Reduction ratio we have on our joints

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM123', bitrate=1000000)

Motor: list[Union[Spectral.SpectralCAN,Spectral.SpectralCAN]] = []
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

Joint: list[Union[SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint,SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint]] = []
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[0], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[0], offset = 0, dir = 0))
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[1], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[1], offset = 0, dir = 0))

timeout_setting = 0.001

initial = 0
initial_setup = [0,0]

# Initialize position values
position_values =  np.array([0.0,0.0])
Motor_values = np.array([0,0])

speed_values = np.array([0,0])

position_send = np.array([0,0])
speed_send = np.array([0,0])
T0 = 0
T1 = 0

received_ids = [0,0] 
Kp = 650
Kd = 0.00550 #  0.0060
Kk = 0.0003 #0.0003

while(1):
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(Position = None,Speed = None, Current = int(T0))
    Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(Position = None,Speed = None, Current = int(T1))

    for i in range(1, 3):  # Loop 9-1=8 to check for received data
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        #print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:

            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            received_ids[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            #print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, position is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            unwrapped_position_raw = Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].unwrap_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)
            Motor_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position
            position_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] =  Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].get_joint_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

            if initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] == 0:
                initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
                Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].determine_sector(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

    # The magic
    T0 = Kp*( position_values[1] -  position_values[0]) + Kd*(Motor[1].speed - Motor[0].speed) - Kk*(Motor[0].speed)
    T1 = Kp*( position_values[0] -  position_values[1]) + Kd*(Motor[0].speed - Motor[1].speed) - Kk*(Motor[1].speed)
    # There are no delays here, we send as fast as possible!

Written with the Spectral Micro

docs.title: What is Gravity Compensation?
docs.text: Gravity compensation is a fundamental concept in robotic control that helps counteract the effects of gravity on a robot's joints and links. By applying the necessary motor current to balance this torque, the robotic joint can remain stationary at any position without additional external forces.

docs.title: Why is it so important?
docs.text:
In robotics, a significant portion of motor power is consumed just fighting against gravity. Gravity compensation algorithms are standard in all industrial robots and collaborative robot arms because they provide: improved position accuracy and control, smoother motion planning, and more precise force control applications.

The gravity compensation algorithm works as a feedforward component to the motor PID control loops, reducing their computational load and improving overall performance.

docs.title: The Approach
docs.text:
In this example, we use the Robotics Toolbox for Python to model a "robotic arm" with a single revolute joint. We compute the required torque using the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA) and convert this torque into a motor current/torque that the motor controller will command the motor.

The full write-up is the blog post Gravity compensation in robotics. The example code is in Gravity compensation in the Python library's examples, with its bill of materials.

import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# Init comms channel 
Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
# Init motor object
Motor1 = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1)

while True:

    # Send this msg to the motor controller, it will respond with position and speed data
    Motor1.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()

    # Get CAN msg, timeout tells us to continue if there is no msg after in this case 0.2 s
    message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.2) 

    # If there was a msg unpack it
    if message is not None:
        print(f"Message is: {message}")
        print(f"Node ID is : {UnpackedMessageID.node_id}")
        print(f"Message ID is: {UnpackedMessageID.command_id}")
        print(f"Error bit is: {UnpackedMessageID.error_bit}")
        print(f"Message length is: {message.dlc}")
        print(f"Is is remote frame: {message.is_remote_frame}")
        print(f"Timestamp is: {message.timestamp}")

        # Here we unpack the data from the packet
        Motor1.UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
        # We are interested in position and speed data that was requested by calling Send_Respond_Encoder_data
        print(f"Motor position is: {Motor1.position}")
        print(f"Motor speed is: {Motor1.speed}")

    else:
        print("No message after timeout period!")
    print("")
    time.sleep(1 )

Building the LEG

In this guide we only recommend you the hardware you can use to build the robot you designed. We do not offer already made designs you can build!

docs.title: Follow a specific trajectory
docs.text:
Joint level control involves directly controlling the angles or positions of the robot's individual joints. Each joint is treated as an independent actuator, and the control system sends commands to each joint to achieve the desired angles.

For this example we will not use joint level control but a different method called Task/Cartesian Level Control. Task or cartesian level control focuses on controlling the position and orientation of the robot's end-effector in a Cartesian coordinate system (X, Y, Z coordinates and orientations).

In our robot leg case we don't have Z axes (or orientation) and our end-effector is foot (end of our robot leg).

In this example we will follow a circle trajectory i X,Y plane. We defined that trajectory with our function generate_circle_coords and with parameters:

  • center - Tuple representing the center coordinates (x, y) in meters
  • radius - Radius of the circle in meters
  • speed - Speed of the end-effector in meters per second
  • time_var - Elapsed time in seconds
Figure 5: The circle the foot traced at speed 1 and at speed 3.

How precise you follow the trajectory depends on the speed you set. With low speeds you can track the circle perfectly. With larger speeds the system can't keep up and overshoots. This is due multiple reaseons like:

  • Inertia and Momentum: At higher speeds, the inertia and momentum of the robot leg increase, making it harder to change directions quickly and accurately.
  • Centrifugal and Coriolis Forces
  • Trajectory Planning and Execution - at higher speeds our trajectory has less points to create a full circle. This is due a fixed rate we send data to our motors eg. every 20ms.
  • Feedforward Control: Lack of proper feedforward control can lead to errors in trajectory tracking, as the controller might not anticipate the required accelerations and decelerations.

You can see that from the example with speed set to 1 and 3.

docs.title: Example code
docs.text:
This code will make your robot leg draw the above circles. It might look complicated but it is not. Once you understand how this example works you can use it as a base for building more complicated projects.

2DOF_leg_demo.py
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import SourceRoboticsToolbox as SourceRoboticsToolbox
import time
import numpy as np
# We are using v1.1.0
from roboticstoolbox import DHRobot, RevoluteDH, ERobot, ELink, ETS
from math import pi, sin, cos
from spatialmath import *
from oclock import Timer, loop, interactiveloop
import math
from typing import Union, Any, List, Optional, cast
INTERVAL_S = 0.02

Needed_joint_pos = np.array([14000,2430]) # These are the positions we got from calib code
Joint_reduction_ratio = [1, 0.90476190] # Reduction ratio we have on our joints

# Setup your CAN coms. Change the channel to match your CAN adapter
Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM6', bitrate=1000000)

# Define our motors
Motor: list[Union[Spectral.SpectralCAN,Spectral.SpectralCAN]] = []
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

# Define the joints
Joint: list[Union[SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint,SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint]] = []
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[0], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[0], offset = -np.pi/2, dir = 0))
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[1], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[1], offset = 0, dir = 0))

timeout_setting = 0.001

initial = 0
initial_setup = [0,0]

testing = 5

# Initialize position values
position_values =  np.array([0.0,0.0])
Motor_values = np.array([0,0])
received_ids = [0,0]

# robot length values (metres)
l = [0.112, 0.1]

alpha_DH = [0,0]

# Create robot model using DH params
L1 = RevoluteDH(a=l[0],d = 0,alpha=alpha_DH[0])
L2 = RevoluteDH(a=l[1],d = 0,alpha=alpha_DH[1])
robot = DHRobot([L1,L2], name="Two link")

prev_pos = np.array([0,0])
speed_var = np.array([0,0])

def generate_circle_coords(center, radius, speed, time):
  """
  Generates x,y coordinates for a circle at a given time, considering constant speed.

  Args:
      center: Tuple representing the center coordinates (x, y) in meters.
      radius: Radius of the circle in meters.
      speed: Speed of the end-effector in meters per second.
      time: Elapsed time in seconds.

  Returns:
      Tuple containing the x and y coordinates in meters.
  """

  # Calculate angular displacement based on speed and time
  angular_displacement = speed * time

  # Use parametric equations for a circle to generate coordinates
  x = center[0] + radius * math.cos(angular_displacement)
  y = center[1] + radius * math.sin(angular_displacement)

  return (x, y)

def save_xy_data(filename, xy_data):
  """
  Saves a list of x,y coordinates to a text file.

  Args:
      filename (str): The name of the text file to save the data to.
      xy_data (list): A list of tuples containing x and y coordinates.
  """

  with open(filename, 'a') as file:
    for x, y in xy_data:
      file.write(f"{x},{y}\n")

# Example usage with update loop (adjust update_interval for your needs)
center = (-0.04, -0.17)
radius = 0.03
speed = 0.8
time_var = 0

# We are using oclock module to generate stable interval defined with INTERVAL_S
timer = Timer(interval=INTERVAL_S, warnings=False, precise=True)
while timer.elapsed_time < 1100000:

    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    #Motor[0].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
    #Motor[1].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
    Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(Position = Needed_joint_pos[0],Speed = speed_var[0], Current = 0)
    Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(Position = Needed_joint_pos[1],Speed = speed_var[1], Current = 0)

    # Handles data we get from the motors
    for i in range(1, 3):  # Loop 9-1=8 to check for received data
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        #print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:

            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            received_ids[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            #print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, position is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            unwrapped_position_raw = Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].unwrap_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)
            Motor_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position
            position_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] =  Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].get_joint_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

            if initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] == 0:
                initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
                Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].determine_sector(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

    # Generate desired x,y coordinates with respect to time_var
    x, y = generate_circle_coords(center, radius, speed, time_var)

    # Create a matrix with those x,y coordinates
    T2 = SE3(x, y, 0)
    # Perform inverse kinematics (get joint data from x,y data)
    q1 = robot.ik_LM(T2, q0 = [-0.8,-1],mask = [1,1,0,0,0,0])
    Needed_joint_pos[0] = Joint[0].get_encoder_position(q1[0][0])
    Needed_joint_pos[1] = Joint[1].get_encoder_position(q1[0][1])  
    speed_var[0] = ((Needed_joint_pos[0] - prev_pos[0]) / INTERVAL_S)
    speed_var[1] = ((Needed_joint_pos[1] - prev_pos[1]) / INTERVAL_S)
    print(speed_var)
    prev_pos[0] = Needed_joint_pos[0]
    prev_pos[1] = Needed_joint_pos[1]
    # Process or visualize the generated coordinates (x, y)
    #print(f"Time: {time_var:.2f}s, Coordinates: ({x:.4f}, {y:.4f})")

    # Update time
    time_var += INTERVAL_S

    t2 = time.perf_counter()
    #print(f"total time is {t2-t1}")

    T = robot.fkine(position_values)
    xy = T.t
    #print(f"{xy[0]},{xy[1]}")
    xy_data = [(xy[0], xy[1])]  # Assuming xy is a single pair of coordinates
    # Save data to a txt file
    save_xy_data('my_data.txt', xy_data)
    #time.sleep(0.05)

docs.title: Plot data
docs.text:
Script that will plot the data of your leg:

plot_leg_data.py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_data(filename):
  """
  Plots data from a text file in the format:
  x1, y1
  x2, y2
  ...

  Args:
      filename (str): The name of the text file containing the data.
  """

  try:
    with open(filename, 'r') as file:
      data = file.readlines()

    x_data = []
    y_data = []
    for line in data:
      # Split the line based on comma (",")
      values = line.strip().split(',')

      # Check if there are exactly two values per line
      if len(values) != 2:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid line format in file '{filename}': {line}")

      try:
        x = float(values[0])
        y = float(values[1])
      except ValueError:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid data type in file '{filename}': {line}")

      x_data.append(x)
      y_data.append(y)

    # Ensure equal x and y scales
    plt.axis('equal')

    # Create the plot
    plt.plot(x_data, y_data)

    # Customize the plot (optional)
    plt.xlabel('X-Position')
    plt.ylabel('Y-Position')
    plt.title('Data Plot from ' + filename)

    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()

  except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Error: File '{filename}' not found.")
  except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")

# Example usage
filename = 'C:\\Users\\xx\\Desktop\\test_code\\env\\Robot_leg\\data_2.txt'  # Replace with your actual filename
plot_data(filename)

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
From the box to a calibrated motor that follows commands, in four parts. The quickest way through is Motor GUI in the browser; every step also shows the terminal commands.

Read first

Reversed supply polarity, a daisy-chain cable the wrong way round, or 5 V on the UART port destroys the driver. The motor turns during calibration. The Safety chapter is two minutes long.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You start from the box: a driver, a motor and the parts below. The wiring needs a multimeter and a soldering iron.

Nothing else is assumed: no experience with motor drivers, a terminal or a program.

docs.title: The four parts
docs.text:
Part What you do What you end with 1. Fit the motor Fit the magnet, mount the board on the motor, solder the coils A driver on its motor, wired 2. Connect Connect the supply and the PC, open Motor GUI or a terminal A driver that talks to your PC 3. Calibrate Restore the defaults, enter the motor's values, calibrate, set the current limit, save A calibrated driver that keeps its settings 4. First moves Turn the motor at a speed, move it to a position, stop it A motor that follows commands

Each step links the page that explains it. Follow the link when a step is not clear or something fails.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Where to get it STEPFOC driver single driver or the starter kit, which has everything below except the motor and the supply A bipolar stepper motor with a rear shaft: NEMA 17, 1 to 5 Ω per coil, 3 A or less the tested motors are safe choices The encoder magnet, diametrically magnetised; the stock one is 6 × 2.5 mm, another thickness is fine if it gives the 1 mm gap magnet A spacer for your motor length and four longer M3 screws printable spacers in Stepper motor accessories USB-to-serial adapter, 3.3 V, and its cable serial adapter, UART cable Power cable power cable A 12 to 29 V supply, 24 V recommended a bench supply with a current limit is the safest start For CAN later: CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter and a CAN cable CAN adapter, CAN cable Optional: 100 kΩ NTC thermistor for motor temperature protection thermistor Software: Motor GUI in Chrome or Edge, or a serial terminal motorgui.com; PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor or the Arduino serial monitor

More: What you need.

docs.title: 1. Fit the motor
docs.text: The driver goes on the back of the motor, over a magnet on the motor's rear shaft.

docs.title: 1. Fit the magnet
docs.text:
1. Press the magnet onto the rear shaft, centred.
  2. Glue it, so that it cannot turn on the shaft.

The magnet must end up about 1 mm above the encoder chip in the middle of the board.

Figure 1: About 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip in the middle of the board.

A magnet that slips is the usual cause of a calibration that "succeeds" and a motor that then runs badly.

Check

The magnet sits centred on the shaft, and once the glue has set it does not move when you push it with a finger. If it does: The encoder magnet.

More: The encoder magnet.

docs.title: 2. Mount the board
docs.text:
1. Remove the motor's four rear screws.
  2. Put the spacer on.
  3. Put the board on the spacer, with the encoder chip towards the magnet.
  4. Put the longer screws in.
  5. Check the gap between the magnet and the encoder chip: 1 mm, not touching.

Check

The board sits parallel to the back of the motor, with about 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip, and the shaft turns by hand without the magnet touching the chip. If not: Mounting on the motor.

More: Mounting on the motor.

docs.title: 3. Wire the motor
docs.text:
1. Find the two coils with a multimeter. The two wires of a coil show a few ohms; wires of different coils show nothing.
  2. Solder one coil to A+ and A−.
  3. Solder the other coil to B+ and B−.

Which coil is which, and which way round, does not matter: calibration detects it.

Figure 2: The motor terminals A+, A−, B+, B− and the other connectors.

Check

With the driver unpowered, a multimeter shows the coil's resistance, a few ohms, between A+ and A− and between B+ and B−, and no strand bridges two pads. If not: Wiring the stepper.

More: Wiring the stepper.

docs.title: 2. Connect
docs.text: The supply powers the motor, the serial adapter connects the PC.

docs.title: 1. Connect power and the PC
docs.text:
1. Connect the supply to a power connector: DC+ to positive, DC− to negative. Check twice.

  2. Connect the serial adapter to the UART connector with the UART cable: TX to RX, RX to TX. 3.3 V only.

    Figure 1: The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.

  3. Power on.

The LED blinks for about two seconds while the bootloader waits for a host. Then the firmware starts, and the LED stays on steadily: the driver is not calibrated yet, which it reports as an error state.

Figure 2: On, steady. The serial adapter alone

The serial adapter alone powers the driver's logic: it answers over UART without the supply, but reports a Vbus error and will not calibrate or move.

More: Power and the CAN daisy chain · Connectors and pinout.

docs.title: 2. Open Motor GUI or a terminal
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal
  1. Open motorgui.com in Chrome or Edge.
  2. Choose the serial connection.
  3. Press Connect, and choose the adapter's port.

Figure 3: Motor GUI connection bar with UART transport, baud rate and Connect.

The driver's identity and state appear: hardware and firmware version, serial number, Not calibrated, No errors.

If nothing connects: the port, the cable's TX/RX, the browser (Web Serial needs a Chromium browser).

More: Motor GUI.

  1. Open a terminal on the adapter's port: 256000 baud, line ending CR+LF.
  2. Type #Info.

The driver prints its hardware and firmware version, its calibration state and the motor parameters. #Error prints the active errors.

More: The serial terminal.

Check

The driver's identity and live state appear before you change settings. A missing connection is covered in Motor GUI or Troubleshooting.

docs.title: 3. Calibrate
docs.text: The driver learns your motor: you give it three values from the datasheet, and calibration measures the rest.

docs.title: 1. Restore the defaults
docs.text:
First the factory defaults, so that calibration does not start from another motor's values or from junk in the EEPROM.

Motor GUITerminal

Press Default in the settings.

#Default
What else #Default resets

It also resets the serial number, hardware version and batch date stored in the EEPROM; from firmware 109 it keeps the CAN node ID.

docs.title: 2. Enter the motor parameters
docs.text:
From the motor's datasheet, for one coil:

  • the pole pairs: 50 for a 1.8° motor, 100 for 0.9°;
  • the phase resistance, in ohms;
  • the phase inductance, in henries (2.6 mH = 0.0026).
Figure 1: The three values on a typical datasheet, here for the 17HS16-2004S1: 1.8°, 1.1 Ω, 2.6 mH.

STEPFOC does not measure these; calibration fails on a value left at 0.

We recommend a Motor GUI preset

In Motor GUI's Presets tab, a preset enters these values for you, with safe limits and gains. For a Source Robotics product, pick its preset. For any other stepper, pick Generic motor and type the pole pairs, the resistance and the inductance from the datasheet: the preset writes them with a low current limit and soft loops, so the motor calibrates safely. More: Motor GUI.

Motor GUITerminal

Enter Pole pairs, Resistance and Inductance in the motor settings and apply them.

#PP 50
#R 1.1
#L 0.0026

Check

#Info prints the values you entered as Number of pole pairs, Single phase resistance and Single phase Inductance (Motor GUI shows them in the motor settings). None of them may be 0.

More: Motor parameters and calibration.

docs.title: 3. Calibrate
docs.text:
1. Fix the motor to the bench, with nothing on the shaft.
  2. Set the supply to 24 V.

  3. Start the calibration:

    Motor GUITerminal

    Start the calibration. The GUI switches to Calibration mode and shows the driver's log step by step.

    #Cal

  4. Keep the shaft free until the end, about a minute more after the log below.

The LED flashes, the motor turns in both directions, and the driver reports each step: the pole pairs, the magnet, the supply, the parameters you entered, the open-loop spin, the angle offset, the motor constants, and finally

Calibration success!
Next, by itself: the encoder table, then anti-cogging (about a minute; keep the shaft free). Everything is saved when they finish (#Encal state, #Cogcal state)
Going to idle!

The driver then goes on to measure the encoder table and the anti-cogging, and saves everything when they succeed.

A failed step names itself, and the log ends with Calibration failed!. Magnet test: Failed is the magnet; Phase order is wrong! means the motor did not turn or did not respond: check the four wires, the supply, and that the magnet does not slip.

Check

The calibration log ends with Calibration success!. If it does not, use the failed step in Calibration troubleshooting; do not treat a stopped motor as success.

More: Motor parameters and calibration, with the whole log and every message.

docs.title: 4. Set the current limit and save
docs.text:
The current limit is the motor's rated phase current in mA. It is 1700 mA after #Default, more than a small motor's rating.

Calibration uses its own 1600 mA for its steps and puts the limit back when it ends, and the encoder table after it runs at 80 % of the limit, so on a small motor set it before you calibrate (step 3); set it now in any case.

Motor GUITerminal

Set the current limit in the limits, then Save (the GUI warns about unsaved changes until you do).

#Ilim 1500
#Save

Without saving, the calibration is gone at the next power cycle. The LED now shows three short flashes and a pause: normal operation.

Figure 2: Three short flashes and a pause.

Check

After Save, Motor GUI no longer marks unsaved changes, and after a power cycle #Info prints Calibrated. Saving explains which settings are kept.

More: Current limit and loop tuning · Saving the configuration.

docs.title: 4. First moves
docs.text: The motor is calibrated and saved. Now it moves on command.

docs.title: 1. Move it
docs.text:
Motor GUITerminal

Use the jog controls:

  • Jog velocity turns the motor at a speed;
  • Jog position moves it to a position;
  • Jog current applies a torque;
  • Send setpoint sends a value in the current control mode.

The plots show position, speed and current while it moves.

Figure 1: Motor GUI simulated motor: device state, controls and live telemetry. 

#V 16384        one revolution per second
#V 0
#P 0            back to where it started
#P 16384        one revolution forward
#Idle

Position is in encoder ticks, 16384 per revolution; speed in ticks per second; current in mA. If the motor hums or whines, lower the current limit or tune the loops.

Check

The position and speed feedback follow the request, and Idle stops driving the motor. A motor that does not follow needs Troubleshooting before a load is attached.

More: Control modes · Current limit and loop tuning.

docs.title: 2. Where to go next
docs.text: You want to Read get to know Motor GUI: the screen, the plots, recordings, several motors Motor GUI, Working in Motor GUI control the driver from a program over CAN Over CAN, then With Python put several drivers on one bus give each a node ID and terminate the ends: Power and the CAN daisy chain protect the motor from overheating Thermistor update the firmware Firmware look up a message or a command API reference understand why it does not work Errors and recovery, Troubleshooting

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: Every CAN message and every UART command of the firmware release this site describes, the defaults the firmware starts with, the error flags, and the map from the Python library's calls to the messages they send.

docs.title: Where the facts come from
docs.text: The command IDs, the frame lengths the firmware accepts, the responses it sends, the list of UART commands with their kind (Set/Get, Get or action), their argument type, the mode each enters and what it prints, the parameter numbers, and the defaults are read from the firmware's source at its release tag by tools/sync_firmware.py in the documentation repository, and the pages are built from that at every build. The descriptions, units and byte layouts are written by hand, and the build fails when they name a command the firmware does not have, or miss one it has, or when a byte layout does not fit the frame. The firmware version is in the version box on the landing page.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Bytes are numbered from 0, the first byte on the bus (data[0]). Multi-byte values are big-endian: the most significant byte first. Floats are IEEE 754 single precision in 4 bytes.
  • Bits inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit: bit 7 is the first flag the firmware packs into the byte, bit 0 the last.
  • Encoder ticks: 16384 per revolution; speeds in ticks per second; currents in mA; voltages in mV.
  • UART command names are case-sensitive and spelled exactly as the firmware compares them.

docs.title: In the API reference
docs.text:
• CAN protocol: the identifier, the three kinds of message, every message by group, and every parameter
  • UART commands: the syntax and every command by group
  • Defaults
  • Errors and LED states
  • Python library: library call → message

docs.title: CAN frame tool and downloads
docs.text: Build or inspect a frame using the command definitions of this manual's firmware release. All calculations run in your browser; the tool does not connect to an adapter or send commands to hardware.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Command definitions (JSON) · Position DBC · Velocity DBC · Current DBC

The JSON includes the firmware tag, source commit, message IDs, every documented layout and its bit order. The DBC files cover nodes 0 to 13, with both the clean and fault-bit identifiers of driver replies. Reserved commands are omitted. Values use the firmware's native units: ticks, ticks/s, mA and the units in the CAN reference.

Choose the DBC for the Send_data_pack_1 layout your host sends:

File Command layout Position DBC 8 bytes: position, speed feedforward, current feedforward Velocity DBC 5 bytes: speed, current feedforward Current DBC 2 bytes: current

The three layouts share a CAN identifier. DBC cannot select a layout from the frame's length, so load the matching file; the browser decoder below handles all three lengths. Other message layouts are the same in each download.

An RTR request uses the same identifier as its data reply. DBC describes the data reply; it does not represent the request's RTR flag or the empty gripper status poll. Both are supported by the browser tool.

The gripper's two object-detection bits have an unusual order: bit 5 is the low bit, bit 4 the high bit. The DBC signal gripper_object_detection_raw retains the wire value and supplies text labels (raw 2 = object while closing, raw 1 = object while opening). The browser decoder converts that pair to the firmware's numeric status (1 = closing, 2 = opening).

docs.title: Try a frame
docs.text:
The example 0x07A, data C8 1E 01 2C C0, is a command to gripper node 0: position 200, speed 30, current 300 mA, activate and action set, E-stop and release direction clear. These are an illustration of the encoding; the device's current and motion limits still apply. Select another message above the fields to build one of its documented forms. To inspect a reply, enter its identifier and data bytes below.

Loading the firmware's command definitions…

Build a frame Node ID (0–13) Message and layout Driver reply has an active fault (error bit 1) Build frame Use this frame in the decoder Decode a frame CAN identifier (hex) Data bytes (hex, up to eight) Remote request (RTR; no payload) Decode frame Enable JavaScript for the frame tool, or use the reference tables and downloads above.

Check

The example decodes to the values above. Change the identifier to 0x1FA to see the same command addressed to node 3. An invalid length or out-of-range field produces an explanation instead of a frame.

For wiring, termination, host timing and recovery, use Over CAN. To look up a message's purpose and accepted lengths, use the CAN reference.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
The settings of the firmware at the release this site describes: their start values in common.h, and what EEPROM.cpp does with each.

  • Start value: the value in common.h. A setting the EEPROM does not keep starts from it at every power-up. A kept setting is replaced at power-up by the value in the EEPROM, so its start value is only seen before that.
  • After #Default: what #Default writes to the EEPROM and loads; — means #Default does not change it.
  • Kept by #Save: whether #Save (Send_Save_config) stores it, so that it survives a power cycle.

Internal state (error flags, counters, calibration steps, scratch variables) is left out; the error flags are in Errors and LED states. A name after a value, such as 160 (CURRENT_BANDWIDTH_DEFAULT), is the constant in constants.h the value comes from. existing_id for the CAN ID means that #Default keeps a valid stored ID (0 when none is stored). The settings of firmware 109 that are parameters, the anti-cogging and the encoder table among them, are in the parameter table with their defaults.
